sections.title: Part 2 — Apropos of the Wet Snow

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 1
paragraphs: * The author of this diary, and the diary itself, are of course imaginary. Even so, it's clear that people like the writer of these notes not only could exist in our society — they have to, given the conditions that shaped us. I've tried to put before the public, more sharply than usual, one of the characters of the recent past. He represents a generation that's still alive. In this first fragment, called "Underground," he introduces himself and his views, and tries, in his way, to explain why he turned out the way he did, and why he had to. The second fragment will contain his actual notes about certain events in his life. — AUTHOR'S NOTE.

I am a sick man.... I am a spiteful man. I am an unattractive man. I think there's something wrong with my liver. But really, I know nothing about my disease, and I'm not even sure what's wrong with me. I don't go to a doctor for it, and never have, though I respect medicine and doctors. Besides, I'm extremely superstitious — superstitious enough to respect medicine, at least (I'm educated enough not to be superstitious, but I am). No, I refuse to see a doctor out of spite. You probably don't get that. Well, I do. Of course, I can't say exactly who I'm punishing with my spite in this case. I know perfectly well that I can't "get back" at the doctors by not seeing them. I know better than anyone that I'm only hurting myself. But still, if I won't go to a doctor, it's out of spite. My liver is bad — fine, let it get worse!

I've been going on like this for a long time — twenty years. I'm forty now. I used to work for the government, but I don't anymore. I was a spiteful clerk. I was rude and enjoyed being rude. I didn't take bribes, you see, so I had to find some other compensation. (That's a weak joke, but I won't cross it out. I wrote it thinking it was witty. Now that I see I was just trying to show off in a cheap way, I won't cross it out — on purpose!)

When people came up to my desk for information, I'd grind my teeth at them, and I'd feel an intense pleasure when I managed to make someone unhappy. I almost always managed it. Most of them were timid people — naturally, since they were petitioners. But of the arrogant ones, there was one officer in particular I couldn't stand. He simply refused to be humble, and he used to clank his sword in this disgusting way. I waged a war with him over that sword for eighteen months. In the end I won. He stopped clanking it. But that was when I was young.

But do you know, gentlemen, what the main thing about my spite was? The whole point — the real sting of it — was that I was constantly aware, even at the height of my bitterest moods, with shame, that I wasn't really spiteful at all, not even truly embittered. I was just scaring sparrows for no reason and amusing myself doing it. I might foam at the mouth, but bring me a doll to play with, give me a cup of tea with sugar in it, and I'd probably calm down. I might even be genuinely moved, though afterwards I'd grind my teeth at myself and lie awake at night for months in shame. That's how I am.

I was lying just now when I said I was a spiteful clerk. I was lying out of spite. I was simply amusing myself with the petitioners and with the officer, and in reality I never could become spiteful. I was aware, every moment, of many other elements in me — completely opposite ones. I felt them positively swarming inside me, these contradictions. I knew they had been swarming in me my whole life, demanding some outlet, but I wouldn't let them out. I wouldn't, deliberately. They tortured me until I felt ashamed of them. They drove me to convulsions and — sickened me, finally, how they sickened me! Now, you're not imagining, gentlemen, that I'm expressing remorse here, asking your forgiveness for something? I'm sure you are.... But I assure you, I don't care if you are....

It wasn't just that I couldn't become spiteful — I didn't know how to become anything: not spiteful, not kind, not a scoundrel, not an honest man, not a hero, not even an insect. Now I'm living out my life in my corner, taunting myself with the spiteful, useless consolation that an intelligent man can't seriously become anything, and that only a fool becomes anything. Yes, a man of the nineteenth century should be — must be, morally — a creature without character. A man of character, an active man, is essentially a limited creature. That's been my conviction for forty years. I'm forty now, and you know forty years is a whole lifetime — it's extreme old age. To live longer than forty is bad manners, vulgar, immoral. Who lives past forty? I'll tell you honestly: fools and worthless people. I'll say it to the face of every old man, every venerable, silver-haired elder! I'll say it to the whole world! I have the right to say it, because I'll go on living to sixty myself. To seventy! To eighty!... Wait, let me catch my breath...

You probably think, gentlemen, that I'm trying to amuse you. You're wrong about that too. I'm hardly the cheerful person you imagine, or might imagine. But if all this chatter has irritated you (and I can feel it has), and you decide to ask me who I am — then my answer is: I'm a collegiate assessor. I worked in the service so I'd have something to eat (and only for that reason). When a distant relative left me six thousand roubles in his will last year, I retired immediately and settled into my corner. I lived in this corner before, but now I've settled into it. My room is a wretched, miserable one on the outskirts of town. My servant is an old peasant woman, ill-natured out of stupidity, and she always smells bad. They tell me the Petersburg climate is bad for me, and that with my modest means it's expensive to live in Petersburg. I know all that better than these wise, experienced advisers and monitors.... But I'm staying in Petersburg. I'm not leaving! I'm not leaving because... oh! Actually, it makes no difference at all whether I leave or not.
But what does a decent man most enjoy talking about?
Answer: himself.
Well then, I'll talk about myself.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Now I want to tell you, gentlemen, whether you want to hear it or not, why I couldn't even become an insect. I tell you solemnly, I've tried many times to become an insect. But I wasn't even up to that. I swear, gentlemen, that being too conscious is an illness — a real, full-blown illness. For everyday human needs, ordinary human consciousness would have been more than enough — that is, half or even a quarter of what falls to a cultivated man of our unhappy nineteenth century, especially one who has the fatal misfortune to live in Petersburg, the most theoretical and intentional city on the entire planet. (There are intentional and unintentional cities.) For example, the kind of consciousness that all so-called direct people and men of action live by would have been quite enough. I'll bet you think I'm writing all this from affectation, to be witty at the expense of men of action. And what's more, that out of bad-mannered affectation I'm clanking my sword like that officer. But, gentlemen, who can really pride himself on his diseases and even swagger about them?

Though, after all, everyone does that. People do pride themselves on their diseases, and I do, perhaps more than anyone. We won't argue about it; my point was absurd. But I'm still firmly convinced that a great deal of consciousness — every kind of consciousness, in fact — is a disease. I stand by that. Let's leave that aside for a moment too. Tell me this: why does it happen that at the very moments when I'm most capable of feeling every refinement of what they used to call "the sublime and the beautiful," it would, as if by design, happen to me not just to feel but actually to do such ugly things — things that... well, in short, things that everyone perhaps does, but which always seemed to come up exactly when I was most aware they shouldn't be done. The more conscious I was of goodness and of "the sublime and the beautiful," the deeper I sank into my mire and the more ready I was to sink in completely. But the main thing was that none of this was accidental in me — it was as if it had to be that way. As if it were my most normal condition, not the slightest bit a disease or a vice. Eventually, all desire to fight against this depravity faded out of me. It ended with my almost believing (perhaps actually believing) that this might be my normal state. But at first, in the beginning, the agonies I went through in that struggle! I didn't believe it was the same with anyone else, and I hid this fact about myself my whole life as a secret. I was ashamed (I'm probably still ashamed, even now). I got to the point of feeling a kind of secret, abnormal, despicable pleasure in returning home to my corner on some disgusting Petersburg night, sharply aware that I'd committed another loathsome action that day, that what was done couldn't be undone, and secretly gnawing, gnawing at myself for it, tearing and consuming myself until at last the bitterness turned into a kind of shameful, accursed sweetness, and finally — into actual, real enjoyment! Yes, into enjoyment, into enjoyment! I insist on it. That's why I brought it up — I keep wanting to know for sure whether other people feel this kind of enjoyment. Let me explain: the enjoyment came precisely from being too acutely conscious of one's own degradation. From feeling that you'd reached the final wall, that it was horrible, but it couldn't be otherwise; that there was no escape; that you could never become a different man; that even if there were still time and faith left for you to change into something different, you most likely wouldn't want to change; or if you did want to, you still wouldn't do anything about it — because in fact there was probably nothing for you to change into.

And the worst of it, the root of it all, was that all of this was in line with the normal, fundamental laws of over-acute consciousness, and with the inertia that follows directly from those laws. So you weren't just unable to change — you couldn't do anything at all. The conclusion of acute consciousness, then, would be that you're not to blame for being a scoundrel — as if that were any consolation to a scoundrel once he's realized he actually is a scoundrel. But enough.... Oh, I've talked a lot of nonsense, but what have I really explained? How is the enjoyment in this to be explained? But I will explain it. I'll get to the bottom of it! That's why I picked up my pen....

I, for example, have a great deal of _amour propre_. I'm as suspicious and easily offended as a hunchback or a dwarf. But honestly, I've sometimes had moments when, if someone had slapped my face, I'd probably have been positively glad of it. I mean it — I'd probably even have found a peculiar enjoyment in it: the enjoyment of despair, of course; but in despair there are the most intense enjoyments, especially when you're acutely aware of how hopeless your position is. And being slapped in the face — well, the consciousness of being ground into pulp would be overwhelming. The worst of it is, look at it any way you like, it always turns out that I was the most to blame for everything. And what's most humiliating is that I'm to blame through no fault of my own — through, so to speak, the laws of nature. First of all, I'm to blame because I'm cleverer than anyone around me. (I've always considered myself cleverer than anyone around me, and sometimes, would you believe it, I've actually been ashamed of it. At any rate, all my life, I've kept my eyes turned aside and never could look people straight in the face.) And finally, I'm to blame because even if I'd had any magnanimity in me, I'd only have suffered more from being aware of how useless it was. I never could have done anything from being magnanimous — neither forgive (because my attacker might have slapped me from the laws of nature, and you can't forgive the laws of nature), nor forget (because even if it were the laws of nature, it's still insulting). And finally, even if I'd wanted to be anything but magnanimous — if I'd wanted, on the contrary, to take revenge on my attacker — I couldn't have taken revenge on anyone for anything, because I'd certainly never have made up my mind to do anything, even if I'd been able to. Why couldn't I have made up my mind? I want to say a few words about that in particular.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 3
paragraphs: How do people who know how to take revenge and stand up for themselves actually do it? When they're seized, let's say, by the feeling of revenge, then for a while there's nothing else in their entire being but that feeling. Such a man simply charges straight at his target like an enraged bull with his horns down, and only a wall will stop him. (By the way: when faced with a wall, men like that — the "direct" people, the men of action — are genuinely stumped. For them, a wall isn't an evasion, the way it is for us, the people who think and therefore do nothing. It's not an excuse for turning aside, an excuse we're always glad to find, even though we hardly believe in it ourselves as a rule. No, they're stumped in all sincerity. The wall has something calming about it for them, something morally soothing, final — maybe even something mysterious... but more about the wall later.)

Well, I consider such a direct person the real, normal man, as kind mother nature wished to see him when she graciously brought him into the world. I envy this man until I'm green in the face. He's stupid, I won't dispute that, but maybe the normal man should be stupid — how do you know? Maybe it's actually beautiful. And I'm even more convinced of this suspicion, if you can call it that, because if you take, for example, the antithesis of the normal man — that is, the man of acute consciousness, who came not from nature's lap but from a retort (this is almost mysticism, gentlemen, but I suspect that, too) — this retort-made man is sometimes so stumped in the presence of his antithesis that, with all his exaggerated consciousness, he genuinely thinks of himself as a mouse, not a man. He may be an acutely conscious mouse, but he's still a mouse, while the other one is a man, and so on, and so on. And the worst of it is that he himself, his own self, looks at himself as a mouse — no one's asking him to, and that's an important point. Now let's look at this mouse in action. Suppose, for instance, that it feels insulted, too (and it almost always feels insulted), and wants to take revenge, too. There may even be a greater accumulation of spite in it than in _l'homme de la nature et de la vérité_. The base, nasty desire to vent that spite on his attacker rankles in him perhaps even more nastily than in _l'homme de la nature et de la vérité_. Because, through his innate stupidity, the latter sees his revenge as straightforward justice; while because of his acute consciousness, the mouse doesn't believe in the justice of it. And so we come to the act itself, the actual revenge. Apart from the one fundamental nastiness, the unfortunate mouse has managed to surround it with so many other nastinesses in the form of doubts and questions, has added so many unsettled questions to the one, that around it inevitably gathers a kind of fatal brew, a stinking mess made up of its doubts, its emotions, and the contempt spat at it by the direct men of action who stand around it solemnly as judges and arbitrators, laughing till their healthy sides ache. Of course the only thing left for it is to wave it all away with its paw and, with a smile of pretended contempt that even it doesn't believe in, creep ignominiously back into its mouse-hole. There, in its nasty, stinking underground home, our insulted, crushed, ridiculed mouse promptly sinks into a cold, malignant, and above all everlasting spite. For forty years on end, it'll remember its injury down to the smallest, most ignominious detail, and every time it'll add still more ignominious details on its own, spitefully teasing and tormenting itself with its own imagination. It'll be ashamed of its imaginings, but yet it'll go over them again and again, every detail, inventing impossible things against itself, pretending these things might happen, and forgiving nothing. Maybe it'll start taking revenge, too, but piecemeal, in trivial ways, from behind the stove, anonymously, without believing in its own right to vengeance or in the success of its revenge — knowing that it'll suffer a hundred times more from all its efforts at revenge than the one it's revenging itself on, who, I dare say, won't even scratch himself. On its deathbed it'll recall it all again, with all the interest accumulated over the years, and...

But it's precisely in that cold, abominable half-despair, half-belief, in that conscious burying of yourself alive for grief in the underworld for forty years, in that acutely felt yet partly doubtful hopelessness of your position, in that hell of unsatisfied desires turned inward, in that fever of vacillations, of resolutions made forever and abandoned again a minute later — that the savor of that strange enjoyment lies, the one I've been talking about. It's so subtle, so hard to analyze, that anyone who's a little limited, or even simply someone with strong nerves, won't understand a single atom of it. "Possibly," you'll add with a grin, "those who've never been slapped in the face won't understand it either," and that way you'll politely hint that I, too, may have had the experience of being slapped at some point in my life, and so I speak as someone who knows. I'll bet that's what you're thinking. But set your minds at rest, gentlemen, I haven't been slapped in the face — though it's a matter of complete indifference to me what you think about it. I may even regret, myself, that I haven't given more slaps in the face during my life. But enough... not another word on a subject of such extreme interest to you.

I'll calmly continue about people with strong nerves who don't understand a certain refinement of enjoyment. Although in certain circumstances these gentlemen bellow their loudest like bulls — and let's suppose this brings them the greatest credit — they nevertheless, as I've said, give in at once when faced with the impossible. The impossible means the stone wall! What stone wall? Why, the laws of nature, of course, the deductions of natural science, of mathematics. As soon as they prove to you, for instance, that you're descended from a monkey, there's no point scowling — accept it as a fact. When they prove to you that in reality one drop of your own fat has to be dearer to you than a hundred thousand of your fellow creatures, and that this conclusion is the final solution of all so-called virtues and duties and other prejudices and fancies, then you just have to accept it. There's no help for it, because two times two is a law of mathematics. Just try refuting it.

"For God's sake," they'll shout at you, "there's no point protesting: it's a case of two times two equals four! Nature doesn't ask your permission, she has nothing to do with your wishes, and whether you like her laws or not, you're bound to accept her as she is, and consequently all her conclusions. A wall, you see, is a wall... and so on, and so on."

Merciful heavens! What do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic, when, for some reason, I dislike those laws and the fact that two times two makes four? Of course I can't break through the wall by smashing my head against it if I really don't have the strength to knock it down. But I'm not going to be reconciled to it just because it's a stone wall and I don't have the strength.

As if a stone wall like that were really a consolation, and really did contain some word of reconciliation, just because it's as true as two times two makes four. Oh, absurdity of absurdities! How much better it is to understand it all, to recognize it all — all the impossibilities and the stone walls — and not to be reconciled to a single one of those impossibilities and stone walls if you find it disgusting to be reconciled. By way of the most inevitable, logical combinations, to reach the most revolting conclusions on the everlasting theme: that even for the stone wall you yourself are somehow to blame, though again it's clear as day that you're not in the least to blame. And so, grinding your teeth in silent impotence, to sink into luxurious inertia, brooding on the fact that there's no one for you even to feel vindictive against — that you have not, and perhaps never will have, an object for your spite, that it's all sleight of hand, a piece of juggling, a card-sharper's trick, that it's simply a mess, no telling what or who, but that despite all these uncertainties and tricks, the ache is still there, and the less you know, the worse the ache.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 4
paragraphs: "Ha, ha, ha! You'll be finding enjoyment in toothache next!" you cry with a laugh.

"Well, even in toothache there is enjoyment," I reply. I had toothache for a whole month, and I know there is. In that case, of course, people aren't spiteful in silence — they moan. But they aren't candid moans; they're malignant moans, and the malignancy is the whole point. The sufferer's enjoyment finds its expression in those moans. If he didn't feel enjoyment in them, he wouldn't moan. It's a good example, gentlemen, and I'll develop it. Those moans express, first of all, the whole pointlessness of your pain, which is so humiliating to your consciousness; the whole legal system of nature, on which you spit disdainfully, of course, but from which you suffer all the same, while she does not. They express the awareness that you have no enemy to punish, but you have pain; the awareness that you are in complete slavery to your teeth, despite all the Wagenheims in the world; that if someone wishes it, your teeth will stop aching, and if he doesn't, they'll go on aching for another three months; and that finally, if you're still defiant and still protesting, all that's left for your own gratification is to flog yourself or to beat your wall with your fist as hard as you can — and absolutely nothing more. Well, these mortal insults, these jeers from someone unknown, end at last in an enjoyment that sometimes reaches the highest degree of voluptuousness. I'm asking you, gentlemen: listen sometimes to the moans of an educated man of the nineteenth century suffering from toothache, on the second or third day of the attack, when he begins to moan not the way he moaned on the first day — that is, not just because he has toothache, not the way some coarse peasant moans, but as a man affected by progress and European civilization, a man who is "divorced from the soil and the national elements," as they say nowadays. His moans become nasty, disgustingly malignant, and go on for whole days and nights. And of course he himself knows that his moans aren't doing him any good. He knows better than anyone that he's only lacerating and harassing himself and others for nothing. He knows that even the audience he's performing for, his whole family, listens to him with loathing, doesn't believe a halfpenny's worth of it, and inwardly understands that he could moan differently, more simply, without trills and flourishes — that he's just amusing himself this way out of ill-humor, out of malignancy. Well, in all these recognitions and disgraces lies a voluptuous pleasure. As if he were saying: "I'm worrying you, I'm tearing your hearts apart, I'm keeping everyone in the house awake. Well, stay awake, then — you, too, can feel every minute that I have toothache. I'm not a hero to you anymore, the way I tried to seem before; I'm simply a nasty person, an impostor. Well, so be it! I'm very glad you see through me. It's nasty for you to hear my despicable moans? Well, let it be nasty; here, I'll let you have a nastier flourish in a minute...." You still don't understand, gentlemen? No, it seems our development and our consciousness must go further before we can understand all the intricacies of this pleasure. You're laughing? Delighted. My jokes, gentlemen, are of course in bad taste — jerky, twisted, lacking in self-confidence. But that's because I have no respect for myself. Can a man of perception have any respect for himself at all?

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Tell me — can a man who tries to find enjoyment in the very feeling of his own degradation possibly have a spark of self-respect? I'm not saying this now from any sentimental kind of remorse. And in fact, I could never bear to say, "Forgive me, Papa, I won't do it again," not because I was incapable of saying that — on the contrary, perhaps just because I was too capable of it, and of doing it convincingly. As if by design, I used to get into trouble in cases when I wasn't to blame in any way. That was the nastiest part of it. At the same time, I was genuinely moved and penitent. I'd shed tears and, of course, deceive myself, even though I wasn't acting in the least, and there was a sick feeling in my heart at the time.... You couldn't even blame the laws of nature for that, though the laws of nature have continually offended me my whole life more than anything. It's loathsome to remember it all, but it was loathsome even at the time. Of course, a minute or so later I'd realize wrathfully that it was all a lie, a revolting lie, an affected lie — all this penitence, this emotion, these vows of reform. You'll ask why I tortured myself with such antics. Answer: because it was very dull to sit with my hands folded, and so I started cutting capers. That's really it. Observe yourselves more carefully, gentlemen, and you'll understand it's so. I invented adventures for myself and made up a life for myself, just so I could at least live in some way. How many times has it happened to me — well, for instance, to take offense simply on purpose, for nothing? You know yourself, of course, that you're offended at nothing, that you're putting it on, but at last you bring yourself to the point of being really offended. All my life I've had an impulse to play such pranks, until at last I couldn't control it. Another time — twice, actually — I tried hard to fall in love. I suffered, too, gentlemen, I assure you. In the depths of my heart there was no faith in my suffering, only a faint stir of mockery, but yet I did suffer, and in the real, orthodox way. I was jealous, beside myself... and it was all from _ennui_, gentlemen, all from _ennui_. Inertia overwhelmed me. You know, the direct, legitimate fruit of consciousness is inertia — that is, conscious sitting-with-the-hands-folded. I've already mentioned this. I repeat, with emphasis: all "direct" people and men of action are active precisely because they're stupid and limited. How to explain that? I'll tell you: because of their limitation, they take immediate and secondary causes for primary ones, and that way they convince themselves more quickly and easily than other people do that they've found an unshakable foundation for their activity. Their minds are at ease — and you know that's the main thing. To begin to act, you have to have your mind completely at ease, with no trace of doubt. How am I, for example, to set my mind at rest? Where are the primary causes for me to build on? Where are my foundations? Where am I to get them from? I exercise myself in reflection, and consequently every primary cause immediately drags another, still more primary one after it, and so on to infinity. That's the very essence of every kind of consciousness and reflection. It must be the laws of nature again. What's the result in the end? The same. Remember, I just spoke about vengeance. (I'm sure you didn't take it in.) I said a man takes revenge because he sees justice in it. So he's found a primary cause — namely, justice. He's at rest on every side, and consequently he carries out his revenge calmly and successfully, convinced he's doing a just and honest thing. But I see no justice in it, I find no virtue in it either, and consequently if I attempt to take revenge, it's only out of spite. Spite, of course, can override everything, all my doubts, and so might serve quite successfully in place of a primary cause — precisely because it isn't a cause. But what to do if I haven't even got spite (which is what I started with, you remember). Once again, because of those accursed laws of consciousness, anger in me is subject to chemical disintegration. You look into it, and the object flies off into thin air, your reasons evaporate, the criminal can't be found, the wrong becomes not a wrong but a phantom — something like a toothache, for which no one is to blame. And so the only outlet left is, again, to beat the wall as hard as you can. So you give up with a wave of the hand, because you haven't found a fundamental cause. Try letting yourself be carried away by your feelings, blindly, without reflection, without a primary cause, pushing consciousness away at least for a time — hate or love, just so as not to sit with your hands folded. The day after tomorrow, at the latest, you'll begin to despise yourself for having knowingly deceived yourself. Result: a soap bubble, and inertia. Oh, gentlemen, do you know — perhaps I consider myself an intelligent man only because all my life I've been able neither to begin nor to finish anything. Granted, I'm a babbler, a harmless, vexing babbler, like all of us. But what's to be done if the direct and sole vocation of every intelligent man is to babble — that is, to pour water through a sieve on purpose?

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 6
paragraphs: Oh, if only I had done nothing simply out of laziness! Heavens, how I'd have respected myself then. I'd have respected myself because I'd at least have been capable of being lazy. There would at least have been one quality, so to speak, positive in me, in which I could have believed. Question: What is he? Answer: A sluggard. How pleasant it would have been to hear that of myself! It would mean that I was positively defined, that there was something to say about me. "Sluggard" — why, it's a calling and a vocation, it's a career. Don't joke, it's true. I'd then be a member of the best club by right, and would find my occupation in continually respecting myself. I knew a gentleman who prided himself all his life on being a connoisseur of Lafitte. He considered this his positive virtue, and never doubted himself. He died not just with a tranquil but with a triumphant conscience, and he was quite right, too. Then I'd have chosen a career for myself: I'd have been a sluggard and a glutton — not a simple one, but, for instance, one with sympathies for everything sublime and beautiful. How do you like that? I've had visions of it for a long time. That "sublime and beautiful" weighs heavily on my mind at forty. But that's at forty. Then — oh, then it would have been different! I'd have found a form of activity in keeping with it: drinking to the health of everything "sublime and beautiful." I'd have seized every opportunity to drop a tear into my glass and then drain it to all that's "sublime and beautiful." I'd have turned everything into the sublime and the beautiful. In the nastiest, most unquestionable trash, I'd have sought out the sublime and the beautiful. I'd have exuded tears like a wet sponge. An artist, for instance, paints a picture worthy of Gay. At once I drink to the health of the artist who painted the picture worthy of Gay, because I love all that is "sublime and beautiful." An author has written _As You Will_: at once I drink to the health of "anyone you will," because I love all that is "sublime and beautiful."

I'd claim respect for doing so. I'd persecute anyone who refused to show me respect. I'd live at ease, I'd die with dignity — why, it's charming, perfectly charming! And what a good round belly I'd have grown, what a treble chin I'd have built up, what a ruby nose I'd have colored for myself, so that everyone, looking at me, would say: "Here is an asset! Here is something real and solid!" And, say what you like, it's very agreeable to hear such remarks about oneself in this negative age.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 7
paragraphs: But these are all golden dreams. Oh, tell me, who was it that first announced, who first proclaimed, that man does nasty things only because he doesn't know his own interests? That if he were enlightened, if his eyes were opened to his real, normal interests, man would at once stop doing nasty things, would at once become good and noble — because, being enlightened and understanding his real advantage, he'd see his own advantage in the good and nothing else, and we all know that no man can knowingly act against his own interests, and consequently, so to speak, by necessity, he'd begin doing good? Oh, the babe! Oh, the pure, innocent child! Why, in the first place, when in all these thousands of years has there ever been a time when man has acted only from his own interest? What are you going to do with the millions of facts that bear witness that men, _consciously_ — that is, fully understanding their real interests — have left them in the background and rushed headlong on another path, to meet peril and danger, compelled by no one and nothing, but, as it were, simply disliking the beaten track, and have obstinately, willfully struck out another, difficult, absurd path, seeking it almost in the dark? So, I suppose, this obstinacy and perversity have been more pleasant to them than any advantage.... Advantage! What is advantage? And will you take it upon yourself to define with perfect accuracy what man's advantage consists of? And what if it sometimes happens that a man's advantage not only may but actually must consist in his desiring, in certain cases, what's harmful to him and not advantageous? And if so, if there can be such a case, the whole principle falls into dust. What do you think — are there such cases? You're laughing; laugh away, gentlemen, but just answer me: have man's advantages been calculated with perfect certainty? Aren't there some that not only have not been included but cannot possibly be included in any classification? You see, you gentlemen have, as far as I know, drawn up your whole register of human advantages from the averages of statistical figures and economic-political formulas. Your advantages are prosperity, wealth, freedom, peace — and so on, and so on. So that the man who, for instance, openly and knowingly went against all that list would, in your view, and certainly in mine too, of course, be an obscurantist or an absolute madman: wouldn't he? But here's what's surprising: why does it happen that all these statisticians, sages, and lovers of humanity, when they reckon up human advantages, invariably leave out one? They don't even take it into account in the form in which it should be taken, and the whole calculation depends on it. There'd be no problem — they'd simply have to take this advantage and add it to the list. But the trouble is that this strange advantage doesn't fall under any classification, and has no place in any list. I have a friend, for example... Oh, gentlemen, but of course he's your friend, too — and indeed there's no one, no one to whom he isn't a friend! When this gentleman prepares for any undertaking, he immediately explains to you, elegantly and clearly, exactly how he must act in accordance with the laws of reason and truth. What's more, he'll talk to you with excitement and passion of the true, normal interests of man; with irony he'll rebuke the short-sighted fools who don't understand their own interests, or the true significance of virtue. And within fifteen minutes, without any sudden outside provocation, but simply through something inside him stronger than all his interests, he'll go off on quite a different tack — that is, act in direct opposition to what he was just saying about himself, in opposition to the laws of reason, in opposition to his own advantage, in fact, in opposition to everything.... I warn you, my friend is a composite character, and so it's hard to blame him as an individual. The fact is, gentlemen, there really must exist something dearer to almost every man than his greatest advantages — or (not to be illogical) there's a most advantageous advantage (the very one that's been omitted, of which we just spoke), more important and more advantageous than all other advantages, for the sake of which a man, if necessary, is ready to act in opposition to all laws — that is, in opposition to reason, honor, peace, prosperity, in opposition to all those excellent and useful things, if only he can attain that fundamental, most advantageous advantage which is dearer to him than all. "Yes, but it's still an advantage," you'll say. But excuse me, I'll make the point clear — and this isn't a case of playing on words. What matters is that this advantage is remarkable precisely because it breaks down all our classifications, and continually shatters every system constructed by lovers of mankind for the benefit of mankind. In fact, it upsets everything. But before I name this advantage to you, I want to compromise myself personally, and so I boldly declare that all these fine systems, all these theories explaining to mankind their real, normal interests so that, inevitably striving to pursue these interests, they might at once become good and noble — are, in my opinion, so far, mere logical exercises! Yes, logical exercises. To maintain this theory of regenerating mankind by means of the pursuit of his own advantage is, in my view, almost the same thing as to claim, for example, following Buckle, that through civilization mankind becomes softer, and consequently less bloodthirsty and less fitted for warfare. Logically it does seem to follow from his arguments. But man has such a predilection for systems and abstract deductions that he's ready to distort the truth on purpose, ready to deny the evidence of his own senses just to justify his logic. I take this example because it's the most glaring instance of it. Just look around: blood is being spilled in streams, and in the merriest way, as if it were champagne. Take the whole nineteenth century, in which Buckle lived. Take Napoleon — the Great, and also the present one. Take North America — the eternal union. Take the farce of Schleswig-Holstein.... And what is it that civilization softens in us? The only gain civilization brings mankind is a greater capacity for variety of sensations — and absolutely nothing more. And through the development of this many-sidedness, man may come to find enjoyment in bloodshed. In fact, this has already happened. Have you noticed that the most civilized gentlemen have been the subtlest slaughterers, men to whom the Attilas and Stenka Razins couldn't hold a candle? And if they're not as conspicuous as the Attilas and Stenka Razins, it's simply because they're so often met with, so ordinary, that they've become familiar to us. In any case, civilization has made mankind, if not more bloodthirsty, then at least more vilely, more loathsomely bloodthirsty. In old days, man saw justice in bloodshed, and with his conscience at peace exterminated those he thought he should. Now we _do_ think bloodshed abominable, and yet we engage in this abomination, with more energy than ever. Which is worse? Decide that for yourselves. They say Cleopatra (excuse an example from Roman history) was fond of sticking gold pins into her slave-girls' breasts and got gratification from their screams and writhing. You'll say that that was in comparatively barbarous times; that these are barbarous times, too, because, comparatively speaking, pins are stuck in even now; that though man has now learned to see more clearly than in barbarous ages, he's still far from having learned to act as reason and science would dictate. But you're fully convinced he'll certainly learn when he gets rid of certain old bad habits, and when common sense and science have completely re-educated human nature and turned it in a normal direction. You're confident that then man will cease from _intentional_ error and will, so to speak, be compelled not to want to set his will against his normal interests. And that's not all: then, you say, science itself will teach man (though to my mind it's a superfluous luxury) that he never really had any caprice or will of his own, and that he himself is something of the nature of a piano-key or an organ-stop, and that besides there are things called the laws of nature; so that everything he does is not done by his willing it, but is done of itself, by the laws of nature. Consequently we only have to discover these laws of nature, and man will no longer have to answer for his actions, and life will become exceedingly easy for him. All human actions will then, of course, be tabulated according to these laws, mathematically, like tables of logarithms up to 108,000, and entered in an index; or, better still, certain edifying works, like encyclopedic dictionaries, will be published, in which everything will be so clearly calculated and explained that there will be no more incidents or adventures in the world.

Then — this is what you say — new economic relations will be established, all ready-made and worked out with mathematical exactitude, so that every possible question will vanish in the twinkling of an eye, simply because every possible answer to it will be provided. Then the "Crystal Palace" will be built. Then... In fact, those will be halcyon days. Of course there's no guarantee (this is my comment) that it won't be, for instance, frightfully dull then (for what will one have to do when everything is calculated and tabulated?), but on the other hand everything will be extraordinarily rational. Of course boredom may lead you to anything. It's boredom that sets people sticking gold pins into others — but all that wouldn't matter. What's bad (this is my comment again) is that I dare say people will be thankful for the gold pins by then. Man is stupid, you know — phenomenally stupid. Or rather he's not at all stupid, but he's so ungrateful that you couldn't find another like him in all creation. I, for instance, wouldn't be in the least surprised if all of a sudden, _à propos_ of nothing, in the midst of general prosperity, a gentleman with an ignoble, or rather with a reactionary and ironic, countenance were to arise and, putting his arms akimbo, say to us all: "I say, gentlemen, hadn't we better kick over the whole show and scatter rationalism to the winds, simply to send these logarithms to the devil, and to enable us to live once more at our own sweet, foolish will!" That again wouldn't matter, but what's annoying is that he'd be sure to find followers — such is the nature of man. And all that for the most foolish reason, which, you'd think, was hardly worth mentioning: that man, everywhere and at all times, whoever he may be, has preferred to act as he chose, and not in the least as his reason and advantage dictated. And one may choose what's contrary to one's own interests, and sometimes one _positively ought_ (that's my idea). One's own free, unfettered choice, one's own caprice, however wild it may be, one's own fancy worked up at times to frenzy — this is that very "most advantageous advantage" we've overlooked, which falls under no classification, and against which all systems and theories are continually being shattered to atoms. And how do these wiseacres know that man wants a normal, a virtuous choice? What has made them imagine that man must want a rationally advantageous choice? What man wants is simply _independent_ choice, whatever that independence may cost and wherever it may lead. And choice, of course — the devil only knows what choice.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 8
paragraphs: “Ha! ha! ha! But whatever you may say about it, choice doesn’t actually exist,” you will interrupt, chuckling. “Science has analysed human beings so thoroughly that we already know choice and so-called freedom of will are nothing more than—”

Wait, gentlemen, I was going to start there myself. I admit I was a little frightened. I was about to say that the devil alone knows what choice depends on, and perhaps that’s a very good thing, but then I remembered what science teaches ... and stopped myself. And now you’ve brought it up. Indeed, if one day someone really discovers a formula for all our desires and whims—explaining what they depend on, the laws that produce them, how they develop, what they aim at in this case or that, and so on, a genuine mathematical formula—then people will probably stop desiring at once; in fact, they certainly will. Who would want to choose by a rule? Besides, a human being would immediately turn into an organ-stop or something similar. What is a person without desires, free will, or choice but a stop in an organ? What do you think? Let’s weigh the chances: could it happen, or couldn’t it?

“H’m!” you conclude. “Our choices generally go wrong because we misunderstand our advantage. Sometimes we choose utter nonsense because we foolishly see it as the easiest way to gain an imagined advantage. But once everything is explained and worked out on paper—and that is entirely possible, since it is contemptible nonsense to suppose some natural laws will remain beyond human understanding—then these so-called desires will certainly disappear. If desire clashes with reason, we shall reason instead of desiring. While keeping our reason, we could not possibly be _senseless_ in our desires, knowingly oppose reason, and wish to harm ourselves. And since every choice and act of reasoning really can be calculated—the laws of our so-called free will will eventually be discovered—joking aside, someone may one day draw up a table of them, and we really shall choose according to it. Suppose they calculate and prove that I thumbed my nose at someone because I couldn’t help doing it, and had to do it in exactly that way. What _freedom_ would remain, especially if I’m an educated man with a degree from somewhere? I could calculate my entire life thirty years ahead. In short, if they arranged this, there would be nothing left for us to do; we would at least have to recognise that. We should tirelessly remind ourselves that, at any given time and under given circumstances, nature doesn’t ask our permission. We have to accept her as she is, not reshape her to suit our fancy. If we really want formulas and tables of rules, and, well, even ... the chemical retort, there’s no getting around it: we must accept the retort too, or it will be accepted without our consent....”

Yes, but this is where I stop! Forgive me for getting so philosophical, gentlemen; forty years underground will do that to you! Let me follow my fancy. Reason is an excellent thing, gentlemen, no argument there, but reason is only reason and satisfies only the rational part of human nature. Will expresses the whole of life, the whole human life, including reason and every impulse. That life, in this expression of itself, may often be worthless, but it is still life, not merely the extraction of square roots. I, for instance, quite naturally want to live to satisfy all my capacities for living, not just my capacity to reason—not just one twentieth of my capacity for life. What does reason know? Only what it has managed to learn. Perhaps there are things it will never learn: poor comfort, but why not admit it frankly? Human nature acts as a whole, with everything in it, consciously or unconsciously, and even when it goes wrong, it lives. I suspect you are looking at me with pity, gentlemen. You tell me again that an enlightened, developed person—in short, the person of the future—cannot knowingly want anything harmful to himself, and that mathematics can prove it. I agree completely: mathematics can. But for the hundredth time, there is one case, just one, in which a person may knowingly and deliberately want something harmful, something stupid, very stupid, simply to have the right to want even something very stupid for himself, without being obliged to want only sensible things. Of course, gentlemen, this very stupidity, this whim of ours, may actually benefit us more than anything else on earth, especially in certain circumstances. It may even be more advantageous than any advantage when it plainly harms us and contradicts reason’s soundest conclusions about our interests. Whatever the circumstances, it preserves what is most precious and important: our personality, our individuality. Some people, you see, insist that this really is humanity’s most precious possession. Choice may agree with reason if it chooses, especially if we don’t abuse it and keep it within bounds. That is useful and sometimes even praiseworthy. Yet very often, indeed most often, choice stubbornly and completely opposes reason ... and ... and ... do you know that this too can be useful, sometimes even praiseworthy? Let’s suppose, gentlemen, that human beings aren’t stupid. Really, we have to suppose it, if only because, if people are stupid, who is wise? But if people aren’t stupid, they are monstrously ungrateful! Phenomenally ungrateful. I believe the best definition of a human being is an ungrateful biped. But that isn’t all, nor even the worst defect. The worst is perpetual moral crookedness, perpetual from the days of the Flood right up to the Schleswig-Holstein period. Moral crookedness, and therefore a lack of good sense: everyone has long accepted that nothing else causes a lack of good sense. Test it: look at human history. What do you see? A grand spectacle? Grand, if you like. Take the Colossus of Rhodes; that alone counts for something. Mr. Anaevsky rightly testifies that some call it the work of human hands, while others claim nature herself created it. Is history colourful? Perhaps that too: take all the military and civilian dress uniforms of every people in every age, and that alone is something. Add the undress uniforms and you’ll never finish; no historian could handle the job. Is it monotonous? Perhaps that too: fighting, fighting, fighting now, fighting at the beginning, fighting at the end—almost too monotonous, you must admit. In short, you can say anything about world history, anything the most deranged imagination might invent. The one thing you can’t call it is rational. The word itself sticks in your throat. And here is the strange thing that keeps happening: moral, reasonable people are forever appearing, sages and lovers of humanity determined to live as morally and rationally as possible throughout their lives. They want, so to speak, to light the way for their neighbours, simply to demonstrate that a moral and rational life is possible in this world. Yet we all know that sooner or later those very people betray themselves with some peculiar trick, often a thoroughly indecent one. So I ask: what can you expect of a being with such strange qualities? Shower him with every earthly blessing, drown him in happiness until only bubbles of bliss remain on the surface. Give him such economic prosperity that he has nothing to do but sleep, eat cakes, and attend to reproducing his species. Even then, from sheer ingratitude and spite, he will play some nasty trick on you. He will risk his cakes and deliberately want the most disastrous rubbish, the most uneconomical absurdity, simply to inject his fatal element of fantasy into all this positive good sense. He will want to keep precisely his fantastic dreams and vulgar folly, simply to prove to himself—as though he needed to—that people are still people, not piano keys. The laws of nature threaten to control those keys so completely that soon we shall be able to want things only according to the calendar. And that’s not all: even if a person really were just a piano key, even if natural science and mathematics proved it, he still wouldn’t become reasonable. From simple ingratitude he would deliberately act perversely, just to make his point. If he couldn’t find the means, he would manufacture destruction and chaos, manufacture every kind of suffering, just to make his point! He would curse the world as only a human being can curse—it is his privilege, the primary difference between him and other animals—and perhaps that curse alone would achieve his aim: convincing himself he is a man, not a piano key! Say that this too can all be calculated and tabulated, chaos, darkness, curses, and that calculating it in advance would itself put a stop to it and restore reason’s rule: then he would deliberately go mad to escape reason and make his point! I believe it, I guarantee it, because humanity’s whole business really seems to be proving to itself every minute that it is human, not a piano key! Even at the cost of its own skin, even through cannibalism! Given all that, how can one resist rejoicing that it hasn’t happened yet, and desire still depends on something we don’t understand?

You will shout at me, if you bother to stoop so low, that nobody is interfering with my free will. All you want is for my will itself, freely and of its own accord, to coincide with my normal interests and with the laws of nature and arithmetic.

Good heavens, gentlemen, what free will can remain once we reach tables and arithmetic, when everything comes down to twice two makes four? Twice two makes four regardless of my will. As though that were what free will meant!

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 9
paragraphs: Gentlemen, I’m joking. I know my jokes aren’t brilliant, but you can turn anything into a joke. Perhaps I’m joking against my own grain. Questions torment me, gentlemen; answer them. You want, for instance, to cure people of their old habits and reform their will according to science and good sense. But how do you know that reforming people this way is not merely possible but _desirable_? What makes you conclude that human inclinations _need_ reform? In short, how do you know this reform would benefit people? To get to the root of it, why are you so utterly convinced that never acting against our real, normal interests, guaranteed by reason and arithmetic, is invariably advantageous and must always be humanity’s law? So far, that is only your assumption. It may be logic’s law, but it isn’t humanity’s. Perhaps you think I’m mad, gentlemen? Let me defend myself. I agree that human beings are creative animals above all, destined to pursue a goal consciously and practise engineering: endlessly, eternally building new roads, _wherever they may lead_. But perhaps people sometimes want to shoot off at a tangent precisely because road-building is their _destiny_. Perhaps, too, even the stupidest “direct” practical man occasionally realises that a road almost always leads _somewhere_, and that where it leads matters less than making it. The main thing is to keep the well-behaved child from despising engineering and sinking into that fatal idleness we all know is the mother of every vice. People like making roads and creating things: no dispute there. But why do they also love destruction and chaos so passionately? Tell me that! I have a word or two of my own on that subject. Perhaps they love chaos and destruction—and no one can deny that sometimes they do—because they instinctively fear reaching their goal and finishing the building they have begun? Who knows, perhaps they love the building only from a distance, not up close at all. Perhaps they love only constructing it and don’t want to live there, leaving the finished place for _les animaux domestiques_, ants, sheep, and so forth. Ants have very different tastes. They possess a marvellous structure of that sort that lasts for ever: the ant-heap.

The respectable race of ants began with the ant-heap and will probably end with it, to the immense credit of their perseverance and good sense. People, however, are frivolous, inconsistent creatures. Perhaps, like a chess player, they love playing the game rather than finishing it. Who knows—no one can say for certain—perhaps humanity’s only earthly goal is this endless process of attainment, life itself, rather than the thing attained. That thing must always be expressed as a formula, as definite as twice two makes four; and such definiteness, gentlemen, is not life but the beginning of death. People have always feared this mathematical certainty, and I fear it now. Granted, a person does nothing but search for it, crosses oceans and sacrifices his life in pursuit; nevertheless, actually succeeding, really finding it, terrifies him, I assure you. He senses that once he finds it, nothing will remain to seek. When workmen finish a job, at least they collect their pay, go to the tavern, then get taken to the police station: there’s something to occupy a week. But where can humanity go? You can see a certain awkwardness when a person achieves such goals. He loves attaining, but isn’t quite pleased to have attained, which is of course absurd. Human beings are comical creatures; the whole affair seems a kind of joke. Still, mathematical certainty is intolerable. To me, twice two makes four is sheer insolence. Twice two makes four is an impudent dandy, hands on hips, blocking your way and spitting. I admit twice two makes four is excellent, but to give everything its due, twice two makes five can sometimes be very charming too.

Why are you so firmly, triumphantly certain that only the normal and positive—only what promotes well-being—is to humanity’s advantage? Might reason be wrong about advantage? Might people love something besides well-being? Perhaps they love suffering just as much? Perhaps suffering benefits them as much as well-being does? People sometimes fall extraordinarily, passionately in love with suffering: that is a fact. No need to consult world history; ask yourself, if you are human and have lived at all. Personally, caring for nothing but well-being strikes me as positively ill-bred. Good or bad, smashing things can sometimes be very pleasant too. I’m not arguing for suffering, or for well-being either. What I defend is ... my whim, and my right to have it guaranteed when necessary. Suffering would be out of place in vaudevilles, for example; I know that. In the “Palace of Crystal” it is inconceivable: suffering means doubt and denial, and what use would a “palace of crystal” be if any doubt about it were possible? Yet I don’t think people will ever give up real suffering—destruction and chaos, that is. Suffering is the sole source of consciousness. I did declare at the beginning that consciousness is humanity’s greatest misfortune, yet I know people treasure it and wouldn’t exchange it for any satisfaction. Consciousness, for instance, is infinitely better than twice two makes four. With mathematical certainty, there is nothing left to do or understand: just bottle up your five senses and sink into contemplation. Keep consciousness, though, and even if you reach the same result, you can at least flog yourself occasionally, which will certainly enliven you. Reactionary though it is, corporal punishment beats nothing.

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 10
paragraphs: You believe in an indestructible palace of crystal, a palace at which you won’t be allowed to stick out your tongue or secretly thumb your nose. Perhaps that is exactly what frightens me about the building: its crystal, its indestructibility, the impossibility of sticking your tongue out at it even when no one is looking.

If it were a hen-house instead of a palace, you see, I might crawl inside to escape the rain. But gratitude for keeping me dry wouldn’t make me call a hen-house a palace. You laugh and say that under those circumstances a hen-house is as good as a mansion. Yes, I reply, if staying out of the rain were the whole purpose of living.

But what if I’ve got it into my head that life has another purpose, and that if one must live, one had better live in a mansion? That is my choice, my desire. You can eradicate it only by changing what I prefer. Well, change it: tempt me with something else, offer another ideal. Until then I won’t mistake a hen-house for a mansion. The palace of crystal may be an empty dream, perhaps incompatible with natural laws, invented merely through my stupidity and my generation’s old-fashioned, irrational habits. Why should that incompatibility matter to me? It makes no difference while the palace exists in my desires—or rather, for as long as those desires exist. Laughing again? Go on, laugh; I’ll endure any ridicule rather than pretend to be full when I’m hungry. One thing I know: you won’t fob me off with a compromise, a recurring zero, merely because it fits the laws of nature and actually exists. I won’t accept, as the crowning fulfilment of my desires, a block of poor people’s tenements on a thousand-year lease, perhaps with a dentist’s sign hanging outside. Destroy my desires, uproot my ideals, show me something better, and I’ll follow. Perhaps you’ll say it isn’t worth your trouble; then I can give exactly the same answer. We’re discussing serious matters. If you won’t grant me your attention, I’ll drop your acquaintance and retreat into my underground hole.

But as long as I live and still have desires, I’d rather my hand withered away than carry a single brick to that building! Don’t remind me that I rejected the palace of crystal merely because I couldn’t stick my tongue out at it. I didn’t say I was especially fond of sticking out my tongue. Perhaps what offended me was that not one of your buildings has ever been immune to it. On the contrary, I’d gratefully let my tongue be cut off if things could be arranged so that I lost every desire to stick it out. It isn’t my fault they can’t be arranged like that and we have to settle for model flats. Why, then, was I made with these desires? Was I put together simply to discover that everything about my construction is a fraud? Is that my entire purpose? I refuse to believe it.

But do you know something? I’m convinced we underground people ought to be kept on a leash. We may spend forty years below ground without speaking, but once we come into daylight and burst out, we talk and talk and talk....

chapters.title: Part 1, Chapter 11
paragraphs: What it all comes down to, gentlemen, is that doing nothing is better! Conscious inertia is better! So hurrah for the underground! I’ve said I envy the normal man with every last drop of bile, but I wouldn’t want to trade places with him as he is now, though I’ll go on envying him. No, no, life underground is more advantageous anyway. There, at least, you can ... Oh, I’m lying even now! I’m lying because I know perfectly well that the better thing isn’t the underground but something else, something utterly different, something I thirst for and cannot find! Damn the underground!

Something else would be better too: if I actually believed any of what I’ve just written. I swear, gentlemen, there isn’t a single thing, a single word in all these pages that I truly believe. Or perhaps I believe it, but at the same time I feel and suspect that I’m lying like a cobbler.

“Then why did you write all this?” you will ask. “I ought to shut you underground with nothing to do for forty years, then visit your cellar and see what stage you’ve reached! How can anyone be left idle for forty years?”

“Isn’t it shameful, humiliating?” you may say, shaking your heads in contempt. “You thirst for life yet try to solve its problems with a tangle of logic. Your attacks are so persistent, so insolent, and all the while you’re terrified! You talk nonsense and enjoy it, make impudent remarks and spend your time panicking and apologising. You say nothing frightens you, yet try to win our approval. You announce that you’re gnashing your teeth, yet struggle to be witty and amuse us. You know your jokes aren’t funny, but plainly admire their literary merits. Perhaps you have really suffered, but you have no respect for your own suffering. You may be sincere, but you lack modesty: the pettiest vanity drives you to expose your sincerity to public disgrace. You surely mean to say something, yet fear makes you hide your final word. You haven’t the courage to speak it, only a coward’s impudence. You boast of consciousness, but don’t trust your own ground. Your mind may work, yet your heart is dark and corrupt, and without a pure heart, full and genuine consciousness is impossible. How intrusive you are, how you insist and pull faces! Lies, lies, lies!”

Of course, I invented every word you say myself. That too comes from underground. For forty years I’ve listened to you through a crack beneath the floor. I made it all up myself; there was nothing else I could invent. No wonder I’ve learned it by heart and it has acquired a literary form....

But are you really gullible enough to think I’ll print this and even let you read it? And another puzzle: why do I call you “gentlemen” and speak as though you really were my readers? Confessions of the kind I intend are never printed or handed to others to read. I’m certainly not strong-minded enough for that, and I don’t see why I should be. But a fancy has taken hold of me, you see, and I want to carry it out at any cost. Let me explain.

Everyone has memories he would share only with friends, not with just anyone. He has other things in his mind he won’t reveal even to friends, only to himself, secretly. Then there are things he is afraid to admit even to himself. Every decent person has a stock of these hidden away; the more decent he is, the larger the stock. Anyway, only recently did I decide to recall some of my early adventures. Until now I always avoided them, with a certain uneasiness even. Now I’m not merely remembering them: I’ve decided to write them down. I want to test whether one can be completely frank even with oneself, without taking fright at the whole truth. Incidentally, Heine says a truthful autobiography is almost impossible, that people are bound to lie about themselves. He thinks Rousseau certainly lied in his confessions, even deliberately, from vanity. I’m convinced Heine is right. I can perfectly understand attributing downright crimes to oneself through sheer vanity; that sort of vanity is entirely imaginable to me. But Heine was judging people who confessed publicly. I’m writing only for myself. Let me state once and for all that if I seem to address readers, it is simply because that form makes writing easier. A form, an empty form: I shall never have readers. I’ve already made that clear ...
I want no restrictions hampering me as I compile these notes. I won’t try to follow a system or method. I’ll write things down as they come back to me.

Perhaps someone will seize on that and ask: if you really don’t expect readers, why make these agreements with yourself, on paper too—that you won’t follow a system or method, that you’ll jot things down as you remember them, and so on and so forth? Why explain yourself? Why apologise?
Well, that’s how it is, I reply.

There’s a whole psychology behind it, though. Perhaps I’m simply a coward. Perhaps I deliberately imagine an audience so that I can carry myself with more dignity while writing. There may be thousands of reasons. And what exactly is my purpose in writing? If it isn’t for the public’s benefit, why not just recall these incidents in my mind instead of putting them on paper?

Quite right; yet on paper it looks more imposing. It has a more impressive air; I can criticise myself better and improve my style. Besides, writing may bring actual relief. Today, for example, one memory from the distant past weighs particularly heavily on me. It returned vividly a few days ago and has haunted me ever since, like an irritating tune you can’t shake. Somehow I must get rid of it. I have hundreds of memories like this, but occasionally one emerges from the hundreds and oppresses me. For some reason I think writing it down might rid me of it. Why not try?
Besides, I’m bored and never have anything to do. Writing will count as a kind of work. They say work makes people kind-hearted and honest. Well, here’s my chance, at least.

Snow is falling today, yellow and grimy. It fell yesterday too, and a few days before that. I think the wet snow brought back the incident I now can’t shake. Let it be a story, then, _à propos_ of the falling snow.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 1
paragraphs: When from dark error’s subjugation My words of passionate exhortation Had wrenched thy fainting spirit free; And writhing prone in thine affliction Thou didst recall with malediction The vice that had encompassed thee: And when thy slumbering conscience, fretting By recollection’s torturing flame, Thou didst reveal the hideous setting Of thy life’s current ere I came: When suddenly I saw thee sicken, And weeping, hide thine anguished face, Revolted, maddened, horror-stricken, At memories of foul disgrace. NEKRASSOV (_translated by Juliet Soskice_).

I was only twenty-four then. Even at that age my life was gloomy, chaotic, and as isolated as a savage’s. I made no friends, deliberately avoided conversation, and buried myself deeper and deeper in my hole. At the office I never looked anyone in the face. I knew perfectly well that my fellow clerks considered me an odd fellow; more than that, they regarded me—or so I always imagined—with a kind of disgust. Sometimes I wondered why I was the only person who imagined that other people found him repulsive. One clerk had a hideous, pockmarked face, a face that positively suggested a criminal. With looks like that, I don’t think I would have dared to meet anyone’s eyes. Another wore such a filthy old uniform that an unpleasant smell surrounded him. Yet neither of these gentlemen showed the slightest embarrassment about his clothes, his face, or anything in his character. It never occurred to either of them that people might look at him with disgust; and if it had, he wouldn’t have cared, provided his superiors didn’t look at him that way. I understand now that my limitless vanity, and the lofty standards I set myself, often made me contemplate myself with a furious dissatisfaction approaching loathing; I then secretly supposed everyone else felt the same. My face, for example: I hated it. I thought it revolting, and even suspected something mean and contemptible in its expression. So every morning, on arriving at the office, I tried to carry myself as independently as I could and to give my face a lofty expression, so that nobody would suspect me of being servile. “My face may be ugly,” I thought, “but at least let it show nobility, expression, and above all, _extreme_ intelligence.” Yet I felt a painful, absolute certainty that my face could never convey any of those things. Worst of all, I thought I actually looked stupid; I would have settled quite happily for looking intelligent. Indeed, I could even have accepted a contemptible face, if people had found it strikingly intelligent at the same time.

Naturally I hated every one of my fellow clerks and despised them all, although I was also, in a way, afraid of them. Sometimes, in fact, I rated them more highly than myself. These changes came over me quite suddenly: one moment I despised them, the next I thought them my superiors. A decent, educated man cannot be vain without demanding terribly much of himself, and without at certain moments despising himself, almost hating himself. But whether I despised them or believed them better than me, I lowered my eyes almost whenever I encountered anyone. I even tried experiments to see whether I could stand so-and-so’s gaze, and I was invariably the first to look away. It drove me almost mad. I also had an unhealthy terror of looking ridiculous, and therefore a slavish devotion to convention in everything outward. I loved keeping to the common rut, and the slightest eccentricity in myself filled me with wholehearted dread. But how could I manage it? I was painfully sensitive, as a man of our age ought to be. They were stupid, every one of them, and as alike as a flock of sheep. Perhaps I alone in the office imagined myself a coward and a slave, and imagined it precisely because I was more developed. Yet it wasn’t just my imagination: I really was one. A coward and a slave. I say so without a trace of embarrassment. Every decent man of our age must be both a coward and a slave. That is his normal state; I am firmly convinced of it. He is built and designed for that very purpose. And this isn’t merely a result of some accidental circumstances today: always, in every age, a decent man has to be a coward and a slave. It is a law of nature for decent people everywhere on earth. If one of them happens to show courage over something, he needn’t congratulate himself or get carried away; over something else he will show the white feather just the same. That is always the inevitable outcome. Only donkeys and mules are brave, and even they are brave only until someone drives them against a wall. They aren’t worth your attention; they really don’t matter at all.
Something else troubled me in those days: nobody was like me, and I was like nobody else. “I am on my own, and they are _everyone_,” I thought, and went on brooding over it.
Clearly, you can see from that how young I still was.

Sometimes everything went the other way. Going to the office could become so disgusting that I often came home feeling ill. Then suddenly, _à propos_ of absolutely nothing, a period of scepticism and indifference would begin—everything came in periods with me—and I would laugh at my own intolerance and finicky standards, and accuse myself of being _romantic_. One moment I wouldn’t speak to a soul; another, I would not only talk to them but actually consider making friends. For no reason whatever, all my fastidiousness would disappear. Who knows? Perhaps I had never really felt it, perhaps it had all been an affectation borrowed from books. I still haven’t settled that question. Once I became quite friendly with them, visited them at home, played preference, drank vodka, discussed promotions.... But allow me to go off the subject here.

Generally speaking, we Russians have never had those foolish, transcendental “romantics,” German and, even more, French, whom nothing can affect. An earthquake might strike, all France might perish on the barricades, and they would remain exactly as they were. They wouldn’t even have the decency to pretend to change; they would keep singing their transcendental songs until their dying hour, because they are fools. We have no fools in Russia; everyone knows that. That is our distinction among foreign nations. Consequently, you don’t find these transcendental characters here in their pure form. The notion that you do comes from the “realistic” journalists and critics of those days, who were always hunting for Kostanzhoglos and Uncle Pyotr Ivanitchs and foolishly taking them for our ideal. They slandered our romantics by treating them as the same transcendental variety found in Germany or France. In fact, our “romantics” have characteristics entirely and directly opposed to that European type; no European measure fits them. (Permit me to use “romantic,” that old-fashioned, highly respected word, familiar to everyone, which has served us so well.) Our romantic’s characteristics are these: he understands everything, _sees everything, and often sees it incomparably more clearly than our most realistic thinkers_; he accepts no person and no thing, while at the same time despising nothing; he gives way and yields for tactical reasons; he never forgets a useful, practical objective—government accommodation free of rent, for instance, pensions, decorations. Through every enthusiasm and every volume of lyric poetry he keeps his eye on that objective. Yet he also keeps “the sublime and the beautiful” untouched inside himself until his dying hour, and incidentally preserves himself like a precious jewel packed in cotton wool, if only for the sake of “the sublime and the beautiful.” Our “romantic” is a man of immense breadth and the biggest rogue among all our rogues, I assure you.... I can assure you from experience, indeed. Provided he is intelligent, of course. But what am I saying! A romantic is always intelligent. I only meant that although we have had foolish romantics, they don’t count; they became foolish only because, in the flower of youth, they degenerated into Germans and settled abroad—preferably in Weimar or the Black Forest—to keep their precious jewel more comfortably.

Take me, for instance. I truly despised my government work, and only refrained from attacking it openly because I did it myself and drew a salary for it. In any case, please note: I didn’t attack it openly. Our romantic would sooner lose his mind—though that very rarely happens—than start denouncing things in public, unless he had another career in prospect. He never gets thrown out. At worst they might carry him off to a madhouse as “the King of Spain,” if he went completely mad. But in Russia only thin, fair-haired people lose their minds. Innumerable “romantics” later rise to considerable rank in the service. What astonishing versatility they have! And what a gift for experiencing the most contradictory feelings! That thought comforted me even then, and I still think the same today. This explains why we have so many “broad natures”: people who keep their ideal even in the deepest degradation. They never lift a finger for it; they are outright thieves and scoundrels; yet they tenderly cherish their original ideal, with tears in their eyes, and remain extraordinarily honest at heart. Yes, only among us can an incurable rogue be absolutely, nobly honest inside, without becoming any less of a rogue. As I say, our romantics often develop into such accomplished rascals—I use “rascals” affectionately—and suddenly reveal such practical knowledge and such a grasp of reality, that their bewildered superiors and the public at large can only gasp in astonishment.

Their versatility really is extraordinary. Heaven knows what it may turn into eventually, and what the future holds for us. There is good material there! I’m not saying this out of some foolish, boastful patriotism. But I feel certain you are once again imagining that I’m joking. Or perhaps you think just the opposite and are convinced I truly believe it. Either opinion, gentlemen, I shall receive as an honour and a particular favour. And please forgive this digression.

Of course my friendship with the other clerks didn’t last. We soon fell out, and in my youthful inexperience I even stopped acknowledging them with a bow, as if I had broken off all relations. That only happened once, though. Usually I was by myself, as always.

For a start, I spent nearly all my time at home with books. I tried to smother the things constantly boiling inside me with impressions from outside. Reading was my only means of getting those impressions. It helped a great deal, of course: it excited me, gave me pleasure, and hurt me. Yet sometimes it bored me terribly. In spite of everything, I craved activity, and would suddenly plunge into sordid, underground, disgusting vice of the most petty kind. My miserable passions burned and stung; my constant, unhealthy irritability brought on hysterical urges, tears, and convulsions. Books were my only resource; that is, nothing in my surroundings attracted me or commanded my respect. Depression overwhelmed me as well.
