I had a hysterical hunger for things that didn’t fit, for contrast, and so I turned to vice. I haven’t been telling you all this to excuse myself.... No, though! That’s a lie. I did want to excuse myself. I make that little observation for my own benefit, gentlemen. I don’t want to tell lies. I promised myself I wouldn’t.

And so at night, secretly, timidly, and alone, I indulged in filthy vice. Shame never left me, even at the most disgusting moments; at those very moments it almost made me curse. Already, even then, I carried my underground world inside my soul. I was terribly afraid that someone would see me, encounter me, recognise me. I went to various out-of-the-way haunts.

One night, passing a tavern, I looked through a lighted window and saw several gentlemen fighting with billiard cues; then one of them was thrown out of the window. Normally I would have found it thoroughly disgusting, but in my mood that night I actually envied the gentleman who had been thrown out. I envied him so much that I went inside the tavern and into the billiard room myself. “Perhaps I can get into a fight too,” I thought, “and they’ll throw me out of the window.”

I wasn’t drunk—but what can you do when depression drives a man into such hysteria? Nothing happened, however. Apparently I wasn’t even good enough to be thrown out of a window. I left without getting the fight I wanted.
Right at the beginning, an officer showed me exactly where I stood.

I was beside the billiard table, innocently blocking the way, when he wanted to get past. He took hold of my shoulders and, without saying a word, without warning me or explaining, shifted me from one place to another and walked on as if he hadn’t noticed me at all. I could have forgiven him for hitting me. I couldn’t forgive being moved without even being noticed.

The devil knows what I would have given for a proper, full-blown quarrel: something more respectable, more _literary_, so to speak. He had treated me like a fly. He stood over six feet tall, and I was a skinny little fellow. Still, I could have started the quarrel myself. I only had to object and they would certainly have thrown me out of the window. Instead I thought better of it and chose to retreat, seething with resentment.

I went straight home from the tavern, bewildered and upset. The following night I went out with the same filthy intentions, even more furtive, more abject, and more miserable than before—with tears in my eyes, as it were. But out I went again all the same. Don’t suppose, though, that cowardice made me creep away from the officer. In my heart I have never been a coward, though in my actions I always have. Don’t rush to laugh at me; I assure you I can explain the whole thing.

Oh, if that officer had only been the kind of man who would agree to a duel! But no: he belonged to that breed of gentlemen—alas, long extinct!—who preferred settling things with billiard cues, or, like Gogol’s Lieutenant Pirogov, calling in the police. They didn’t fight duels; in any case they would have considered a duel with a civilian like me utterly improper. To them, duelling itself was something impossible, something French and freethinking. They were perfectly willing to bully people, though, especially when they stood over six feet tall.

It wasn’t cowardice that made me slink off; it was boundless vanity. I wasn’t frightened of his six feet, or of a good thrashing, or of being thrown out of the window. I would have had enough physical courage for that, I assure you. What I lacked was moral courage. I feared that everyone there, from the insolent billiards marker to the lowest little clerk with his pimples, his stink, and his greasy collar, would jeer without understanding me when I began to protest and speak in literary language. Among us, you can discuss a point of honour—not honour itself, but the point of honour, the _point d’honneur_—only in literary language. Ordinary speech simply cannot accommodate a “point of honour.” I knew with absolute certainty—what a grasp of reality, for all my romanticism!—that they would split their sides laughing. And the officer wouldn’t merely beat me, that is, beat me without insulting me: he would certainly jab his knee into my back, kick me round the billiard table, and only then, perhaps, take pity on me and drop me out of the window.

Naturally, with me such a trivial incident couldn’t stop there. Afterwards I often encountered the officer in the street and watched him very closely. I can’t be certain he recognised me; from various signs I think he didn’t. But I—I stared at him with malice and hatred, and this went on ... for years! With every year my resentment deepened. First I started quietly making inquiries about him. That wasn’t easy, since I knew nobody. But one day, while I followed him at a distance as if I were tied to him, I heard someone call out his surname in the street. That was how I learned his name. Another time I trailed him home and paid the porter ten kopecks to tell me where he lived, which floor, whether alone or with others, and so on: everything, in fact, a porter could tell me. One morning, though I had never attempted to write anything, I suddenly thought of composing a satirical novel about this officer to expose his villainy. I wrote it with relish. I exposed his villainy all right, even exaggerated it. At first I changed his surname just enough to leave it easily recognisable, but then thought better of it and changed it altogether, and sent the story to the _Otetchestvenniya Zapiski_. Attacks of that kind weren’t fashionable then, however, and the story wasn’t printed. That upset me enormously.

Sometimes resentment actually seemed to choke me. Finally I decided to challenge my enemy to a duel. I composed a splendid, enchanting letter, begging him to apologise and hinting fairly unmistakably at a duel if he refused. I arranged the letter so that, if the officer had possessed the slightest understanding of the sublime and the beautiful, he would surely have thrown his arms round my neck and offered me his friendship. How wonderful that would have been! How well we would have got along! “His superior rank could have protected me, and I could have developed his mind with my culture, and, well ... my ideas; all sorts of things could have followed.” Just imagine: two years had passed since his insult, and my challenge would have been absurdly out of date, despite all the ingenuity with which the letter concealed and explained away that awkward fact. But thank God—to this day I thank the Almighty with tears in my eyes—I never sent it. Even now, thinking what might have happened if I had sent it makes a cold shiver run down my spine.

Then suddenly I took my revenge in the simplest possible way, through a flash of genius! A brilliant idea came to me. On holidays I sometimes went walking on the sunny side of the Nevsky at about four in the afternoon. Walking is hardly the word: it was an endless succession of miseries, humiliations, and resentments. No doubt that was precisely what I wanted. I wriggled along in a most undignified way, like an eel, constantly stepping aside for generals, officers of the guards and hussars, or ladies. At those moments my heart would contract painfully, and heat would run down my back at the mere thought of my miserable clothes and my wretched, cringing little figure as it scurried along. It was regular martyrdom, an unending, unbearable humiliation. The thought became a constant physical sensation: in the eyes of this whole world I was only a fly, a nasty, disgusting fly. More intelligent, more developed, more sensitive and refined than any of them, of course, but a fly nevertheless, forever giving way to everyone, insulted and injured by everyone. Why did I torture myself like this? Why did I go to the Nevsky? I don’t know. I simply felt drawn there whenever I had the chance.

Even then I was beginning to feel a surge of the pleasure I described in the first chapter. After the affair with the officer, the place attracted me more strongly than ever. I met him most often on the Nevsky, and there I could admire him. He too went there mainly on holidays. He too stepped out of the way of generals and people of high rank, and wriggled between them like an eel. But people like me, or even people better dressed than me, he simply walked over. He came straight at them as if the space ahead were empty, and never, in any circumstances, moved aside. Watching him, I savoured my resentment and ... always made way for him, full of resentment. It infuriated me that even out in the street I couldn’t meet him on equal terms.

“Why do you always have to be the one who steps aside first?” I kept asking myself in a hysterical fury, sometimes waking at three in the morning. “Why you, instead of him? There’s no regulation saying so, no written law. You should both give way equally, as civilised people normally do when they meet. He moves halfway, you move halfway, and you pass one another with mutual respect.”

But nothing of the sort ever happened. I always gave way, and he didn’t even notice that I was doing it. Then, lo and behold, a brilliant idea struck me! “Suppose,” I thought, “I meet him and don’t step aside? Suppose I deliberately refuse to move, even if I bump into him? What then?” The sheer audacity of the idea seized me and wouldn’t let me rest. I dreamed about it incessantly, horribly, and deliberately went to the Nevsky more often, to picture more clearly exactly how I would do it when the moment came. I was delighted. The plan seemed more and more workable, more and more possible.

“Of course I won’t actually shove him,” I thought, already feeling kinder in my delight. “I’ll simply hold my course and collide with him, not very hard: our shoulders will just knock together, no more than decency allows. I’ll push against him exactly as much as he pushes against me.” At last I decided once and for all. But the preparations took a very long time. First, I would need to look a little more respectable when carrying out my plan, so I had to think about my appearance. “If anything goes wrong—some sort of public scandal, for instance, and the people there are the most _recherché:_ the Countess walks there, Prince D. walks there, the entire literary world is there—I must be properly dressed. That commands respect, and in itself makes us equals in society’s eyes.”

With that in mind, I requested an advance on my salary and bought black gloves and a respectable hat at Tchurkin’s. Black gloves struck me as both more dignified and more _bon ton_ than the lemon-coloured pair I had originally considered. “That colour is too flashy; it makes you look as if you want to attract attention.” So I rejected the lemon-coloured gloves. I had long since prepared a good shirt with white bone studs. Only my overcoat held me up. In itself it was an excellent coat and kept me warm, but it was padded and had a raccoon collar, the very height of vulgarity. Whatever the sacrifice, I had to replace that collar with beaver, like an officer’s. I began making trips to the Gostiny Dvor, and after several visits chose a piece of cheap German beaver. German beaver soon gets shabby and looks dreadful, but when new it looks extremely good, and I needed it only for this occasion. I asked the price: even this was too expensive. After thinking it through carefully I decided to sell the raccoon collar. For the rest—a considerable amount for me—I decided to ask Anton Antonitch Syetotchkin for a loan. He was my immediate superior, an unassuming man, though serious and sensible. He never lent anybody money, but when I entered the service the influential person who obtained my post had specially recommended me to him. I was horribly anxious. Borrowing from Anton Antonitch seemed something monstrous and disgraceful. For two or three nights I couldn’t sleep. In fact I was sleeping badly throughout that period; I was feverish, with a vague sinking sensation in my chest, or else a sudden throbbing, throbbing, throbbing! First Anton Antonitch looked surprised, then he frowned, then he considered it. In the end he lent me the money, taking a written authorisation to deduct the amount from my salary two weeks later.

At last everything was ready. The handsome beaver had replaced the shabby-looking raccoon, and I gradually began putting the plan into action. It wouldn’t do to act casually, at random; I had to manage it skilfully, by degrees. But I admit that after repeated attempts I began to despair: we simply couldn’t collide. I would prepare everything and make up my mind absolutely; it seemed we were about to run straight into each other—and before I knew what I was doing, I had stepped aside again and he had passed without noticing me. As I approached him, I even prayed that God would give me resolution. Once I had fully resolved to do it, but ended by stumbling and falling at his feet. At the very last instant, when I was six inches away, my courage deserted me. He stepped over me quite calmly, while I shot off to one side like a ball. That night I was ill again, delirious and feverish.

Then all at once it ended gloriously. The night before, I had decided to give up my fatal scheme and abandon the whole thing. With that purpose I went to the Nevsky for the last time, simply to see how I would abandon it. Suddenly, three paces from my enemy, I unexpectedly made my decision: I shut my eyes, and we crashed together at full speed, shoulder against shoulder! I never moved an inch, and passed him as his perfect equal! He didn’t even turn his head; he pretended not to notice. But it was only pretence, I am certain of that. I am certain of it to this very day! Of course I came off worse, since he was stronger, but that wasn’t what mattered. What mattered was that I had achieved my purpose, maintained my dignity, refused to yield a single step, and publicly established my social equality with him. I came home feeling fully avenged for everything. I was delighted, triumphant; I sang Italian arias. Naturally I won’t describe what happened to me three days later. If you have read my first chapter, you can guess. Later the officer was transferred, and I haven’t seen him for fourteen years now. What is the dear fellow doing these days? Who is he walking over?

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Eventually, though, my spell of dissipation would end, and afterwards I always felt terribly ill. Remorse followed; I tried to push it away, because I felt too sick already. Gradually I grew accustomed to that as well. I grew accustomed to everything—or rather, I willingly resigned myself to putting up with it. But I had one escape that reconciled everything: refuge in “the sublime and the beautiful,” in dreams, naturally. I was an appalling dreamer. I would spend three months dreaming without a break, tucked into my corner, and you may believe me when I say that at such times I bore no resemblance to the gentleman whose fluttering chicken heart drove him to put a German beaver collar on his overcoat. Suddenly I was a hero. If my six-foot lieutenant had come to visit, I wouldn’t even have let him in. At such moments I couldn’t so much as picture him standing before me. What did I dream, and how did those dreams satisfy me? It is hard to explain now, but they satisfied me then. Indeed, even now they satisfy me to some extent. They were particularly sweet and vivid after a bout of dissipation: they arrived with remorse and tears, with curses and ecstasies. I had moments of such intoxicating happiness that, on my honour, there wasn’t the slightest trace of irony in me. I had faith, hope, love. At such times I believed blindly that some miracle, some event from outside, would suddenly make all this open up and expand. A prospect of suitable activity would appear before me—something beneficial, good, and above all _ready-made_. What sort of activity I couldn’t have said; the essential thing was to have it all prepared for me. Then I would emerge into daylight, almost riding a white horse, crowned with laurel. I could imagine myself in no position except the foremost, and for precisely that reason I was perfectly content to occupy the lowest in actual life. A hero or a creature crawling in the mud: nothing in between. That was what ruined me. In the mud, I consoled myself by remembering that at other times I was a hero, and the hero became a cloak for the mud. An ordinary man disgraced himself by getting dirty; a hero stood too high to be completely soiled, and therefore could allow himself to get dirty. Notice, too, that these visitations of “the sublime and the beautiful” came even during my dissipation, at the very moments when I touched bottom. They arrived in separate bursts, as if to remind me they existed, but their arrival never drove the dissipation away. On the contrary, the contrast seemed to give it extra relish; they were present just enough to provide an appetising sauce. That sauce consisted of contradictions and suffering, of agonising self-examination. All those pangs and pinpricks gave my dissipation a certain sharpness, even a significance; they did the work of an appetising sauce perfectly. There was a certain depth of meaning in it. I could hardly have resigned myself to a clerk’s simple, vulgar, straightforward debauchery, or tolerated all its filth. What would have attracted me to it then, and drawn me out into the streets at night? No, I had a lofty escape from the whole business.

And what tenderness I felt sometimes in those dreams—oh Lord, what loving kindness! In those “flights into the sublime and the beautiful,” although the love was imaginary, although I never directed it towards any actual human being, there was so much of it that afterwards I didn’t even feel an impulse to put it into practice. That would have been unnecessary. Everything slid agreeably, through an idle, enchanting transition, into the realm of art: into beautiful patterns of life lying ready for use, mostly stolen from poets and novelists and adapted to every sort of purpose and need. I, for instance, triumphed over everyone. They all lay in dust and ashes, of course, compelled to acknowledge my superiority spontaneously, and I forgave them all. I became a poet and a great gentleman; I fell in love. I inherited countless millions and immediately devoted them to humanity. At the same time I publicly confessed my shameful deeds, which naturally weren’t merely shameful but contained a great deal of “the sublime and the beautiful,” something in the style of Manfred. Everybody kissed me and wept—what idiots they would have been otherwise—while I went hungry and barefoot, preaching new ideas and winning an Austerlitz against the obscurantists. Then the band played a march, an amnesty was proclaimed, and the Pope agreed to leave Rome and retire to Brazil. Then all Italy attended a ball at the Villa Borghese on the shores of Lake Como; for the occasion Lake Como was moved to the neighbourhood of Rome. Then came a scene in the bushes, and so on, and so on—as if you didn’t know all about it yourselves. You will say it is vulgar and contemptible to drag all this before the public, after the tears and ecstasies I have just admitted. But why contemptible? Do you imagine I am ashamed of it all, or that it was stupider than anything in your own lives, gentlemen? I assure you some of these fantasies were by no means badly put together.... They didn’t all happen on Lake Como’s shores. Still, you are right: it really is vulgar and contemptible. The most contemptible thing is that I am now trying to defend myself to you. More contemptible even than that is my making this very observation. But enough, or we shall never finish; each step will be more contemptible than the one before....

I could never endure more than three months of continuous dreaming before an irresistible longing to plunge into society overcame me. By plunging into society I mean visiting my superior at the office, Anton Antonitch Syetotchkin. He was the only lasting acquaintance I ever had in my life; the fact amazes even me now. But I visited him only when that particular phase came on, when my dreams had grown so blissful that I urgently needed to embrace my fellow creatures, the whole of humanity. For that purpose I required at least one human being who actually existed. Unfortunately Anton Antonitch received visitors on Tuesdays, so I always had to arrange for my passionate desire to embrace humanity to fall on a Tuesday.

Anton Antonitch lived on the fourth floor of a house in Five Corners, in four low-ceilinged rooms, each smaller than the last, all with a particularly pinched, yellowish appearance. His two daughters lived with him, along with their aunt, who poured the tea. The girls were thirteen and fourteen, both snub-nosed; they made me terribly shy because they were forever whispering and giggling together. Their father generally sat in his study on a leather couch in front of the table, with some grey-haired gentleman, usually a colleague from our office or another department. I never saw more than two or three visitors there, always the same people. They discussed excise duty, senate business, salaries, promotion, His Excellency and how best to please him, and so forth. I had the patience to sit beside them like a fool for four hours at a time, listening, unable to think of anything to say and not daring to utter a word. I grew dazed; several times I felt sweat breaking out; a sort of paralysis took hold of me. Yet it was pleasant, and did me good. Once home again, I put off my desire to embrace all humanity for a while.

I did have one other acquaintance of sorts: Simonov, an old schoolfellow. There were actually quite a few former schoolfellows in Petersburg, but I had nothing to do with them and had even stopped nodding to them in the street. I believe I transferred to my department simply to escape their company and cut every connection with my hateful childhood. A curse on that school and on all those dreadful years of penal servitude! In any case, I broke with my schoolfellows as soon as I entered the world. Two or three remained to whom I still nodded in the street. Simonov was one of them. At school he had never stood out in any way; he was quiet and even-tempered. But I had detected a certain independence in his character, even honesty, and I don’t suppose he was particularly stupid either. Once I had shared some rather soulful moments with him, though they didn’t last long and somehow suddenly clouded over. He was obviously uncomfortable remembering them, and I think he always feared I might resume that tone. I suspected he disliked me, but since I wasn’t entirely sure, I kept visiting him.

So on one occasion, when solitude had become unbearable, I remembered Simonov. It was Thursday, and I knew Anton Antonitch’s door would be closed. As I climbed to Simonov’s fourth floor, I thought how the man disliked me and how wrong it was to visit him. But such reflections always seemed deliberately to push me into an awkward position, so I went in. Almost a year had passed since I last saw him.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 3
paragraphs: Two more of my old schoolfellows were there when I arrived. They appeared to be discussing something important. They scarcely noticed me coming in, which was strange, since I hadn’t seen them for years. Evidently they considered me about as significant as an ordinary fly. Even at school they hadn’t treated me like that, although they all hated me. Of course I knew they must now despise me for having got nowhere in the service, and for sinking so low, wearing shabby clothes and so forth: to them these things proved my incompetence and insignificance. But I hadn’t expected contempt on this scale. Simonov seemed genuinely surprised that I had come. Even in the old days my visits had always seemed to surprise him. All this threw me off balance. I sat down rather miserably and began listening to their conversation.

They were earnestly and excitedly discussing a farewell dinner for the next day. Their friend Zverkov, an army officer, was leaving for a distant province. Zverkov too had been at school with me throughout. In the upper classes I had begun to hate him particularly intensely. In the lower ones he had merely been a handsome, lively boy whom everybody liked. Yet I had hated him even then, precisely because he was handsome and lively. He was always poor at his lessons and grew steadily worse, but graduated with a good certificate thanks to powerful connections. In his final year he inherited an estate with two hundred serfs; since nearly all the rest of us were poor, he began to swagger among us. He was extremely vulgar, but good-natured too, even in his swaggering. Despite our shallow, fantastic, make-believe notions of honour and dignity, nearly all of us positively crawled before Zverkov; the more he swaggered, the more they crawled. They weren’t hoping to gain anything: they did it simply because nature had favoured him. Besides, it was somehow accepted among us that Zverkov was an authority on tact and social grace. That last point infuriated me most. I hated his abrupt, self-assured voice and the pleasure he took in his own jokes, often appallingly stupid, though boldly expressed. I hated his handsome, stupid face—though I would gladly have exchanged my intelligent one for it—and his easy military manners, so fashionable in the ’forties. I hated hearing him talk about his future conquests of women: he didn’t dare begin his campaign until he had an officer’s epaulettes, and impatiently awaited them. I hated his boasting about the duels he would constantly fight. I remember once attacking him suddenly, though I was usually so silent. He was chatting with schoolfellows during a free moment about his future dealings with the fair sex; growing as playful as a puppy in sunshine, he declared that he wouldn’t overlook a single village girl on his estate. That was his _droit de seigneur_; if the peasants dared complain, he would have them all whipped and double their tax, the bearded scoundrels. Our servile rabble applauded. I attacked him, not out of pity for the girls or their fathers, but simply because they were applauding such an insect. I got the better of him that time, but stupid as Zverkov was, he was quick and impudent. He laughed it off in a way that left my victory incomplete: the laughter was on his side. Several times afterwards he got the better of me, though casually, jokingly, without malice. I stayed angrily, contemptuously silent and refused to answer. When we left school he made friendly approaches; flattered, I didn’t reject them, but we soon drifted apart quite naturally. Later I heard of his success in the barracks as a lieutenant and of the wild life he led. Then other rumours came, about his progress in the service. By then he had begun ignoring me in the street; I suspected he feared compromising himself by greeting someone so insignificant. Once I saw him at the theatre, in the third tier of boxes. By that time he wore shoulder-straps. He kept twisting and turning, making himself agreeable to an aged General’s daughters. In three years his looks had deteriorated considerably, although he was still rather handsome and polished. You could see that by thirty he would be fat. This, then, was the Zverkov for whom my schoolfellows planned a farewell dinner. They had kept in touch with him throughout those three years, although privately, I am convinced, they didn’t regard themselves as his equals.

One of Simonov’s visitors was Ferfitchkin, a Russianised German: a little fellow with a monkey’s face, a blockhead forever mocking everyone, and my bitter enemy since the lower classes. Vulgar, insolent, and full of swagger, he pretended to an exquisitely sensitive sense of personal honour, although at heart, of course, he was a miserable little coward. He was among those admirers of Zverkov who cultivated him for personal advantage, and often borrowed money from him. The other visitor, Trudolyubov, was quite unremarkable: a tall young army man with a cold expression, reasonably honest, but a worshipper of success in any form, who could think of nothing except promotion. He was some distant relation of Zverkov’s, which, absurdly enough, gave him a certain standing among us. He had always considered me entirely insignificant. His treatment of me, though hardly polite, was tolerable.
“Well, at seven roubles apiece,” Trudolyubov said, “that makes twenty-one from the three of us. We should get a decent dinner for that. Naturally Zverkov won’t contribute.”
“Naturally he won’t; we’re the ones inviting him,” Simonov ruled.

“Can you really imagine,” Ferfitchkin broke in, excited and full of himself, like an insolent footman boasting about his General’s decorations, “can you imagine Zverkov allowing us to pay for everything? He’ll accept out of tact, but he’ll order six bottles of champagne.”
“Would the four of us want six bottles?” Trudolyubov asked, noticing only the number of bottles.
“Then it’s the three of us, with Zverkov making four: twenty-one roubles, Hôtel de Paris, tomorrow at five,” Simonov concluded. They had put him in charge of the arrangements.
“Why twenty-one roubles?” I asked, a little agitated and making a show of offence. “With me included, surely the amount is twenty-eight roubles, not twenty-one.”
I imagined that inviting myself so abruptly, so unexpectedly, would seem positively graceful. It would win them all over immediately, I thought, and make them regard me with respect.
“Do you want to come as well?” Simonov asked without any sign of pleasure, apparently avoiding my eyes. He understood me through and through.
The very completeness of his understanding made me furious.
“Why shouldn’t I? I believe I went to school with him too. And I confess it hurts me that you’ve left me out,” I said, beginning to boil over once more.
“Where were we supposed to find you, then?” Ferfitchkin interrupted rudely.
“You and Zverkov never got along,” Trudolyubov added with a frown.
But by this time I had seized on the idea and refused to let it go.

“I don’t see that anyone has the right to judge that,” I retorted, my voice trembling as though something momentous had occurred. “Perhaps the fact that we haven’t always got along is precisely why I want to come now.”
“Oh, nobody can understand you ... and all your subtleties,” Trudolyubov sneered.
“We’ll include you, then,” Simonov decided, turning to me. “The Hôtel de Paris, tomorrow at five o’clock.”
“And the money?” Ferfitchkin began quietly, motioning towards me as he addressed Simonov. But he stopped, because even Simonov looked embarrassed.
“That’s enough,” Trudolyubov said, rising. “If he’s so eager to join us, let him come.”
“But this is something private, just among friends,” Ferfitchkin said irritably, picking up his hat as well. “It isn’t an official function.”
“Perhaps we don’t want it at all ...”

They left. Ferfitchkin gave me no farewell at all, and Trudolyubov scarcely nodded. Left _tête-à-tête_ with me, Simonov looked irritated and bewildered, and gave me a strange look. He neither sat down nor invited me to sit.
“H’m ... yes ... tomorrow, then. Will you give me your share now? I’m only asking so I know,” he muttered awkwardly.
I went crimson. At that instant I remembered the fifteen roubles I had owed Simonov for ages—though really I had never forgotten the debt, despite never repaying it.
“You realise, Simonov, I couldn’t possibly have known when I came here.... I’m terribly annoyed with myself for forgetting....”
“All right, all right, it doesn’t matter. Tomorrow after dinner will do. I only wanted to know.... Please don’t...”
He stopped speaking and began walking up and down, even more irritated. As he paced, he started stamping his heels.
“Am I holding you up?” I asked after we had stood silent for two minutes.
“Oh!” He gave a start. “Well—to tell the truth—yes. I have to visit someone ... quite near here,” he added apologetically, looking rather ashamed.
“Good heavens, why didn’t you tell me?” I cried, snatching up my cap with an astonishingly casual air, the very last manner I would have expected from myself.

“It’s just nearby ... hardly two steps away,” Simonov repeated. He escorted me to the front door with a fussiness entirely unlike him. “Tomorrow at five, precisely,” he called after me down the stairs. He was delighted to have got rid of me. I was furious.

“What got into me? Whatever made me force myself on them?” I wondered, striding down the street and grinding my teeth. “All for a scoundrel, a pig like Zverkov! Of course I’d better stay away. Of course I should simply snap my fingers at them. I’m under no obligation. I’ll post Simonov a note tomorrow....”
What maddened me, however, was knowing for certain that I would go: I would insist on going. The more tactless and improper my presence would be, the more certain it was that I would turn up.

There was a practical obstacle as well: I had no money. I possessed just nine roubles, and seven were due to my servant Apollon as his monthly wages. That was all I paid him; he had to provide for himself.
Given his character, failing to pay was impossible. But I shall speak of that fellow, that plague of my life, another time.
All the same, I knew I would go, and would withhold his wages.

I had the most dreadful dreams that night. No wonder: all evening memories of my miserable schooldays had weighed on me, and I couldn’t shake them off. Distant relatives, on whom I depended and of whom I have heard nothing since, had sent me to that school. They sent a silent, desolate boy, already crushed by their reproaches, already tormented by doubts, looking at everyone with fierce suspicion. My schoolfellows greeted me with cruel, malicious taunts because I was different from them all. I couldn’t bear their mockery; I couldn’t submit with the shameful readiness with which they submitted to one another. I hated them from the beginning and shut myself away in timid, wounded, excessive pride. Their coarseness revolted me. They laughed cynically at my face and my awkward figure; yet what stupid faces they had themselves. At our school there seemed to be something that particularly made boys’ faces deteriorate and grow stupid. So many handsome boys came to us! Within a few years they became repulsive. Even at sixteen I watched them in gloomy amazement; already the smallness of their thoughts and the stupidity of their interests, games, and conversations astonished me. They failed to understand such essential things, and ignored such striking, impressive subjects, that I couldn’t help considering them beneath me. Wounded vanity wasn’t what drove me to that conclusion. For God’s sake don’t force on me those worn-out remarks, repeated until they make one sick, that “I was only a dreamer,” whereas they already understood life. They understood nothing; they had no conception of real life. I swear that was what angered me most. On the contrary, they approached the plainest, most striking realities with fantastic stupidity, and even then they had learned to worship success. Anything just that was oppressed or despised they mocked with shameful heartlessness. They confused rank with intelligence. At sixteen they were already discussing comfortable posts. Much of this, of course, came from their stupidity and from the bad examples that had surrounded them throughout childhood and boyhood. They were monstrously depraved. Much of that too was superficial, a pose of cynicism; of course youth and freshness sometimes showed through even their depravity. But even that freshness was unattractive: it appeared as a kind of rakish swagger. I hated them terribly, though perhaps I was worse than any of them. They returned my feelings and made no attempt to hide their dislike. By then I no longer wanted their affection. On the contrary, I constantly yearned to humiliate them. To escape their ridicule I deliberately worked as hard as I could at my studies and forced my way to the top. That impressed them. Gradually they also realised I had already read books none of them could read, and understood things outside our school curriculum that they had never even heard of. They responded with vicious sarcasm, but inwardly they were impressed, especially when the teachers began noticing me for these reasons. The mockery stopped; the hostility stayed. Our relations settled into permanent coldness and strain. Eventually I couldn’t stand it. As I grew older I developed a hunger for company, for friends. I tried making friends with some of my schoolfellows, but somehow any intimacy between us was always strained and soon died of its own accord. Once I actually had a friend. But I was already a tyrant inside: I wanted unlimited power over him. I tried to teach him contempt for his surroundings and demanded that he break with them completely and disdainfully. My passionate affection frightened him. I drove him to tears, to hysterics. He was a simple, devoted soul, but the instant he gave himself to me entirely I began hating him and pushed him away. It was as if I had needed him only to conquer him, to bring him under my power, and nothing more. But I couldn’t conquer all of them; my friend was unlike the others too, a rare exception, in fact. On leaving school, my very first act was to abandon the particular career intended for me, so as to sever every tie, curse my past, and shake its dust from my feet.... And after all that, heaven knows why I should go trudging over to Simonov’s!

Early the next morning I woke and sprang excitedly out of bed as if everything were about to happen that instant. I believed some fundamental change in my life was approaching and would inevitably arrive that day. Perhaps because outside events were so rare for me, even the smallest one always made me feel that my life was about to change completely. Nevertheless I went to the office as usual, then slipped home two hours early to prepare. The crucial thing, I thought, was not to arrive first; otherwise they would suppose I was overjoyed to be invited. But there were thousands of crucial details like that, all agitating and overwhelming me. I polished my boots a second time myself. Nothing on earth would have persuaded Apollon to clean them twice in one day; he considered that beyond his duties. I stole the brushes from the passage, carefully avoiding his notice because I feared his contempt. Then I examined my clothes in minute detail. Everything seemed old, worn, threadbare. I had let myself become far too slovenly. My uniform might be neat, but I couldn’t go to a dinner in uniform. Worst of all, a large yellow stain marked the knee of my trousers. I had a foreboding that it would rob me of nine-tenths of my personal dignity. I also knew how pitiful it was to think that. “But there’s no time for thinking now: this is the real thing,” I told myself, and my heart sank. Even then I knew perfectly well how monstrously I was exaggerating everything. But what could I do? I couldn’t control myself; I was already shaking with fever. In despair I pictured the cold, disdainful reception that “scoundrel” Zverkov would give me; the dull, impenetrable contempt in the blockhead Trudolyubov’s look; the insolent rudeness with which that insect Ferfitchkin would snigger at me to win Zverkov’s favour. Simonov would understand everything and despise my cringing vanity and lack of courage. Worst of all, the whole scene would be so petty, so _unliterary_, so commonplace. Clearly the best course was not to go at all. But that was the least possible course of all: whenever I feel driven to do something, it is as if I am being pitchforked into it. I would have mocked myself for ever afterwards: “So you lost your nerve, lost your nerve, ran away from the _real thing!_” Instead, I passionately wanted to show that whole “rabble” that I wasn’t nearly as spineless as I seemed to myself. What is more, even in the worst fit of that cowardly fever, I dreamed of gaining the upper hand, dominating them, sweeping them away, winning their affection, if only through my “lofty thoughts and unmistakable wit.” They would desert Zverkov; he would sit to one side, silent and ashamed, while I crushed him. Then perhaps we would make peace and drink to everlasting friendship. But the bitterest, most humiliating fact was that even then I knew, fully and certainly, that I had no real need for any of this. I didn’t actually want to crush them, subdue them, or attract them; even if I succeeded, I didn’t truly care a straw about the result. Oh, how I prayed for the day to hurry past! In unspeakable anguish I went to the window, opened the little movable pane, and looked into the troubled darkness and the thickly falling wet snow. At last my miserable little clock wheezed out five. I snatched up my hat and tried not to look at Apollon. He had expected his monthly wages all day, but was too foolishly stubborn to mention them first. Slipping between him and the door, I jumped into a fine sledge, spent my last half-rouble on the fare, and arrived in grand style at the Hôtel de Paris.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 4
paragraphs: The day before, I had been certain I would arrive first. But arriving first wasn’t the problem. Not only was nobody there; I could hardly even find our room. The table hadn’t been set. What did it mean? After asking the waiters a great many questions, I discovered that dinner had been ordered for six, not five. They confirmed this at the buffet too. I became positively ashamed of continuing to ask. It was only twenty-five past five. If they had changed the time, they might at least have told me—that was what the post was for—instead of making me ridiculous in my own eyes and ... and even in the waiters’ eyes. I sat down. A servant began setting the table, and his presence humiliated me still more. Towards six they brought candles, although lamps were already burning in the room. Yet when I arrived it hadn’t occurred to the waiter to bring the candles immediately. In the next room two gloomy, angry-looking men were eating silently at separate tables. Farther away another room was full of noise, even shouting. A crowd was laughing; nasty little shrieks came in French: there were ladies at that dinner. It was sickening, really. I have rarely spent such unpleasant moments. So when they all arrived together, precisely at six, I was overjoyed to see them, as if they had come to rescue me. I even forgot that I ought to show resentment.

Zverkov came in first, clearly the leader. They were all laughing, Zverkov included. On seeing me, however, he straightened a little and approached me at a deliberate pace, with a slight, rather jaunty bow from the waist. He shook my hand in a friendly way, but not too friendly, displaying the guarded courtesy of a General, as if extending his hand served to fend something off. I had expected just the opposite: he would enter, burst into his usual thin, shrill laugh, and start making his feeble jokes and clever remarks. I had been preparing for those since yesterday. I hadn’t expected this condescension, this courtesy of a high official. So he considered himself indescribably superior to me in every respect! If he simply meant to insult me with that official manner, it wouldn’t matter, I thought; I could find some way to repay him. But suppose this sheep’s head really believed himself my superior, without the least wish to offend, and therefore could regard me only patronisingly? The mere possibility took my breath away.

“I was surprised when I heard you wanted to join us,” he began with a lisping drawl, something new for him. “You and I seem never to see each other. You keep away from us. You shouldn’t, you know. We aren’t as dreadful as you imagine. Anyway, I’m glad we’re renewing our acquaintance.”
Then he turned casually away to put his hat on the windowsill.
“Have you waited here long?” Trudolyubov asked me.
“I came at five, the time you gave me yesterday,” I answered loudly, with an irritation on the verge of exploding.
“Didn’t you let him know we’d changed the time for dinner?” Trudolyubov asked Simonov.
“No. I forgot,” Simonov answered without any trace of regret. He went to order the _hors d’œuvres_ without so much as apologising to me.

“You’ve been waiting here an entire hour? Oh, you poor fellow!” Zverkov exclaimed mockingly; in his view this was bound to be wonderfully funny. That scoundrel Ferfitchkin chimed in with his nasty little snigger, like a yapping puppy. He too thought my situation exquisitely ridiculous and embarrassing.
“There’s nothing funny about it!” I shouted at Ferfitchkin, growing angrier and angrier. “It wasn’t my fault. It was other people’s. They failed to tell me. It was ... it was ... simply absurd.”
“Absurd, and something more,” Trudolyubov muttered, innocently taking my side. “That’s too mild a word. It was plain rudeness—unintentional, naturally. Still, how could Simonov ... h’m!”
“If someone had played that sort of trick on me,” Ferfitchkin remarked, “I would have ...”
“You ought to have ordered something for yourself,” Zverkov broke in, “or just asked them to serve your dinner without waiting for us.”
“You’ll agree I could have done that without your permission,” I snapped. “If I chose to wait, it was ...”

“Sit down, gentlemen,” Simonov called as he returned. “Everything’s ready. I can vouch for the champagne; it’s beautifully chilled.... You see, I didn’t have your address. Where could I look for you?” He suddenly turned towards me, but again appeared to avoid meeting my eyes. Plainly he resented something. It must have been yesterday’s business.
Everyone sat, and so did I. The table was round: Trudolyubov to my left, Simonov to my right, Zverkov opposite me, and beside Zverkov, between him and Trudolyubov, Ferfitchkin.
“Tell me, are you ... working in a government office?” Zverkov continued his attentions. Seeing my embarrassment, he honestly believed he should be pleasant to me and, so to speak, lift my spirits.
“Is he trying to make me throw a bottle at his head?” I thought furiously. These unfamiliar surroundings left me unnaturally quick to take offence.
“At the N—— office,” I replied in a broken voice, staring down at my plate.
“And is it a go-od po-ost? Tell me, why di-id you leave the job you started in?”

“Why I di-id was because I wanted to leave the job I started in,” I said, drawing my words out even more than he did, barely controlling myself. Ferfitchkin burst into a loud laugh. Simonov gave me an ironic look. Trudolyubov stopped eating to watch me curiously.
Zverkov flinched, but tried to pretend he hadn’t noticed.
“And what is the pay?”
“The pay for what?”
“I mean your sa-a-lary, of course?”
“Why are you interrogating me?” Nevertheless I immediately told him how much I earned. My face went horribly red.
“Not a particularly generous sum,” Zverkov remarked with grandeur.
“You certainly can’t dine in cafés on that kind of money,” Ferfitchkin added insolently.
“I’d call that very little indeed,” Trudolyubov observed seriously.
“And you’ve become so thin! You look so different!” Zverkov added, a touch of poison in his voice, inspecting me and my clothes with something like insolent pity.
“Oh, don’t make him blush,” Ferfitchkin cried with a snigger.

“My dear sir, let me inform you that I am not blushing,” I finally burst out. “Do you understand? I am eating here, in this café, at my own expense, not someone else’s. Please note that, Mr. Ferfitchkin.”
“Wha-at? Isn’t everyone sitting here paying for his own dinner? You seem to be ...” Ferfitchkin rounded on me, turning lobster-red, and glared furiously straight into my face.
“Tha-at,” I answered, aware I had gone too far, “and I think we might do better to discuss something a little more intelligent.”
“So you’re planning to parade your intelligence before us, are you?”
“Don’t worry yourself; that would be completely out of place in this company.”
“What are you chattering on about like that, my good sir, eh? Has sitting in your office driven you mad?”
“That’s enough, gentlemen, enough!” Zverkov shouted commandingly.
“What a stupid business!” Simonov muttered.

“It is stupid, certainly. We’ve come together as friends to give a comrade a farewell dinner, and you start a quarrel,” Trudolyubov said, rudely directing his remarks only at me. “You invited yourself along, so don’t spoil everyone’s evening.”
“Enough, enough!” Zverkov cried. “Stop it, gentlemen; this isn’t the occasion. Let me tell you instead how I almost got married the day before yesterday....”

There followed a farcical account of how this gentleman had nearly married two days earlier. Nothing was actually said about the marriage. Instead, generals, colonels, and kammer-junkers adorned the story, with Zverkov almost the leading figure among them. Everyone laughed approvingly; Ferfitchkin practically squealed.
Nobody gave me any attention, and I sat there crushed with humiliation.

“Good God, these aren’t my sort of people!” I thought. “And what a fool I’ve made of myself in front of them! Still, I let Ferfitchkin go too far. The brutes think it’s an honour for me to sit at their table. They don’t realise the honour is theirs, not mine! I’ve got thinner! My clothes! Oh, damn these trousers! Zverkov spotted the yellow mark on the knee the instant he walked in.... But what does it matter! I must stand up now, this very second, take my hat, and leave without saying a word ... contemptuously! Tomorrow I can issue a challenge. The scoundrels! As if seven roubles mattered to me. They might imagine.... Damn it! I don’t care about those seven roubles. I’m leaving right now!”

Naturally I stayed. In my humiliation I drank glass after glass of sherry and Lafitte. I wasn’t used to drinking, and it soon affected me. As the wine rose to my head my irritation grew. Suddenly I wanted to insult them all outrageously, then leave; to catch the right moment and show what I was capable of, so they would say, “He’s clever, even if he is ridiculous,” and ... and ... oh, damn every one of them!

I inspected them insolently through sleepy eyes, but they seemed to have forgotten I existed. They were cheerful, loud, full of talk. Zverkov talked constantly. I began to listen. He was describing some exuberant lady whom he had finally induced to declare her love—lying like a horse, of course—and how his close friend Prince Kolya, a hussar officer with three thousand serfs, had helped him in the affair.
“And yet this Kolya with his three thousand serfs hasn’t bothered to turn up tonight to say goodbye to you,” I suddenly interrupted.

For a moment everyone fell silent. “You’re drunk already.” At last Trudolyubov condescended to notice me, throwing a contemptuous glance my way. Zverkov studied me silently as if I were an insect. I looked down. Simonov hurriedly refilled the glasses with champagne.
Trudolyubov lifted his glass; everyone followed his example except me.
“To your health, and a good journey!” he cried to Zverkov. “To the old days, and to our future, hurrah!”
They emptied their glasses and crowded round Zverkov to kiss him. I stayed where I was, my full glass untouched in front of me.
“Well, aren't you going to drink?” Trudolyubov bellowed, losing his patience and turning towards me threateningly.
“I intend to give a separate speech, on my own behalf ... then I shall drink, Mr. Trudolyubov.”
“What a spiteful brute!” Simonov muttered. I straightened in my chair and grasped my glass feverishly, preparing for something extraordinary, although I didn’t really know what I meant to say.
“_Quiet!_” Ferfitchkin shouted. “We’re about to hear something witty!”
Zverkov waited with great seriousness, knowing what to expect.
“Lieutenant Zverkov,” I began, “allow me to say that I hate empty phrases, the people who spout them, and men in corsets ... that’s point one, and point two comes next.”
Everyone stirred in their seats.

“My second point: I hate filthy jokes and the people who tell them. Especially the people who tell them! Third: I love justice, truth, and honesty.” I was speaking almost automatically now, beginning to shudder in horror myself, with no idea how I had come to be saying such things. “I love thought, Monsieur Zverkov; I love genuine comradeship, between equals, not ... H’m ... I love ... Still, why not? I’ll drink to your health as well, Mr. Zverkov. Seduce the Circassian girls, shoot the fatherland’s enemies, and ... and ... your health, Monsieur Zverkov!”
Zverkov rose from his chair, made me a bow, and replied:
“I am deeply indebted to you.” He was dreadfully offended, and his face turned pale.
“Damn the man!” Trudolyubov roared, slamming his fist onto the table.
“He deserves a punch in the face for that,” Ferfitchkin shrieked.
“We should throw him out of here,” Simonov muttered.

“Not another word, gentlemen; nobody move!” Zverkov cried solemnly, restraining their collective indignation. “I thank you all, but I’m quite capable of showing him myself exactly how little I value his words.”
“Mr. Ferfitchkin, tomorrow you will answer for what you just said!” I declared loudly, turning towards him with dignity.
“You mean a duel? Certainly,” he replied. But I must have looked so ridiculous issuing a challenge, so utterly unsuited to the part, that everyone, Ferfitchkin included, doubled up with laughter.
“Yes, leave him alone, of course! He’s completely drunk,” Trudolyubov said disgustedly.
“I’ll never forgive myself for allowing him to come,” Simonov muttered once more.

“Now’s the moment to throw a bottle at their heads,” I told myself. I picked up the bottle ... and poured another glass.... “No, I’d better stay until the end,” my thoughts continued. “You’d like me to leave, my friends. Nothing will make me go. I’ll deliberately sit here drinking until the very end, to show that I consider you utterly insignificant. I’ll stay and drink because this is a public house and I’ve paid my entrance money. I’ll sit drinking because to me you’re nothing but pawns, lifeless pawns. I’ll sit here and drink ... and sing if I feel like it. Yes, sing, because I have every right to ... to sing ... H’m!”

But I didn’t sing. I merely tried to avoid looking at any of them. I arranged myself in the most unconcerned poses and waited impatiently for them to speak _first_. Alas, they never spoke to me! And oh, how desperately, how desperately I wanted at that moment to make peace with them! Eight struck, and finally nine. They left the table for the sofa. Zverkov stretched out on a lounge and rested one foot on a round table. Wine was brought over; he did, in fact, order three bottles at his own expense. Naturally they didn’t invite me to join them. They clustered round him on the sofa and listened almost reverently. Clearly they were fond of him. “Why? Why?” I wondered. Now and then drunken enthusiasm overcame them and they kissed one another. They discussed the Caucasus, the nature of genuine passion, comfortable government posts, and the income of a hussar named Podharzhevsky. None of them knew him personally, but they rejoiced that he had so much money. They spoke of Princess D.’s extraordinary grace and beauty, although none had ever seen her. Then they arrived at Shakespeare’s immortality.

With a contemptuous smile I began pacing the opposite side of the room, facing the sofa, from table to stove and back again. I did everything possible to demonstrate that I could manage without them, yet deliberately made my boots noisy, thumping my heels. All in vain: they paid no attention. I had the patience to pace before them from eight until eleven, over the very same stretch, table to stove, stove to table. “I’m walking up and down for my own pleasure, and nobody can stop me.” The waiter occasionally came in and paused to stare. All that turning made me rather dizzy; at moments I thought I was delirious. Three times during those three hours I became drenched in sweat and dried off again. Sometimes a sharp, piercing thought stabbed my heart: ten years would pass, twenty, forty, and even in forty years I would remember these moments, the filthiest, most ridiculous, most dreadful of my life, with disgust and humiliation. Nobody could have worked harder to degrade himself so shamelessly. I understood that completely, completely, yet I kept pacing from the table to the stove. “Oh, if you only knew the thoughts and feelings I’m capable of, how cultivated I am!” I sometimes thought, mentally addressing the sofa where my enemies sat. But they behaved as though I weren’t in the room. Once, just once, they turned towards me. Zverkov was discussing Shakespeare, and I suddenly laughed contemptuously. My laugh was so artificial and disgusting that they all stopped talking and watched me silently, solemnly, for two minutes as I paced from table to stove, _ignoring them_. But nothing happened. Nobody spoke, and after two minutes they stopped noticing me again. The clock struck eleven.
“My friends,” Zverkov cried, rising from the sofa, “it’s time we all went off _there!_”

“Yes, of course, of course,” the others agreed. I turned sharply towards Zverkov. I was so tormented and exhausted that I would have cut my throat to end it. Fever burned in me; sweat-soaked hair clung to my forehead and temples.
“Zverkov, I ask your forgiveness,” I said abruptly, decisively. “Yours too, Ferfitchkin, and everyone’s, everyone’s. I’ve insulted every one of you!”
“Aha! You don’t fancy a duel, then, old fellow,” Ferfitchkin hissed spitefully.
A sharp pain shot straight through my heart.

“No, Ferfitchkin, I’m not afraid of the duel! I’m willing to fight you tomorrow, after we make peace. In fact I insist, and you cannot refuse. I want to prove I have no fear of a duel. You can fire first; I’ll fire into the air.”
“He’s trying to console himself,” Simonov remarked.
“He’s just talking delirious nonsense,” Trudolyubov said.
“Just let us through. Why are you standing in our way? What is it you want?” Zverkov replied contemptuously.
All their faces were flushed and their eyes bright; they had drunk a great deal.
“I’m asking for your friendship, Zverkov. I insulted you, but ...”
“Insulted? _You_, insult _me?_ Understand this, sir: under no circumstances could you ever possibly inflict an insult on _me_.”
“That should be enough for you. Move aside!” Trudolyubov finished.
“Olympia belongs to me tonight, friends; that’s settled!” Zverkov cried.
“We won’t challenge your claim, we won’t challenge it,” the others replied, laughing.
I stood there feeling as though they had spat on me. They left the room noisily, Trudolyubov launching into some stupid song. Simonov stayed a moment to tip the waiters. Suddenly I approached him.
“Simonov! Lend me six roubles!” I said with desperate determination.
He stared at me in utter astonishment, his eyes blank. He was drunk as well.
“Surely you don’t mean to come along with us?”
“Yes.”
“I haven’t any money,” he snapped, and left the room with a contemptuous laugh.
I grabbed hold of his overcoat. It was like a nightmare.

“Simonov, I saw you had money. Why won’t you lend it? Am I a scoundrel? Be careful before you refuse. If only you knew, if you knew why I’m asking! Everything in my future, every plan I have, depends on it!”
Simonov took out the money and practically threw it in my face.
“Take it, then, if you’ve no shame!” he said mercilessly, and ran after the others.

For a moment I was alone: the mess, the leftovers of dinner, a broken wineglass on the floor, spilled wine, cigarette ends; alcohol fumes and delirium in my head, agonising misery in my heart. And finally the waiter, who had seen and heard everything, staring curiously into my face.
“I’m going there!” I shouted. “Either they all get on their knees and beg for my friendship, or I slap Zverkov across the face!”

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 5
paragraphs: “So here it is, here it is at last—an encounter with real life,” I muttered, rushing headlong down the stairs. “A very different thing from the Pope leaving Rome for Brazil, very different from that ball beside Lake Como!”
“You’re a scoundrel if you laugh about this now,” a thought suddenly flashed across my mind.
“What does it matter!” I shouted back at myself. “Everything is ruined now!”
There was no sign of them anywhere, but it made no difference: I knew where they had gone.

A lone night sledge-driver stood by the steps in a rough peasant’s coat, dusted with the wet, almost warm snow that was still falling. The air was hot and steamy. His shaggy little piebald horse was covered in snow too, and coughing; I remember that distinctly. I rushed towards the roughly built sledge. But just as I lifted my foot to climb in, remembering how Simonov had handed me those six roubles seemed to fold me in half, and I collapsed into the sledge like a sack.
“No, it will take a great deal to make up for all that,” I cried. “But I’ll do it, or die on the spot tonight. Get going!”
We began moving. Everything in my head was spinning round.

“They won’t fall on their knees and beg for my friendship. That’s an illusion, a cheap, disgusting, romantic fantasy: another ball on Lake Como. So I have to slap Zverkov’s face! I’m obliged to do it. That settles it, then: I’m flying there to slap his face. Faster!”
The driver pulled hard on the reins.

“I’ll do it the instant I enter. Should I say a few words first, before the slap? No. I’ll simply walk in and hit him. They’ll all be sitting in the drawing room, and he’ll be on the sofa with Olympia. That damned Olympia! Once she laughed at my appearance and rejected me. I’ll pull her hair and tug Zverkov’s ears! No, one ear would be better; I’ll drag him round the room by it. Perhaps they’ll all start beating me and throw me out. In fact that’s the likeliest outcome. Never mind! I’ll have slapped him first, anyway; I’ll have taken the initiative, and under the laws of honour that counts for everything. He’ll carry the stain, and no beating can wipe it away: nothing can except a duel. He will have to fight. Let them beat me now, then. Let them, the ungrateful wretches! Trudolyubov will hit hardest, since he’s so strong; Ferfitchkin will certainly creep in from the side and pull my hair. But never mind, never mind! That’s what I’m going for. Finally the blockheads will have to recognise the tragedy of it all! While they drag me to the door, I’ll shout that in reality they aren’t worth my little finger. Faster, driver, faster!” I shouted at him so savagely that he jumped and flicked his whip.

“We’ll fight at dawn; that’s decided. No more office for me. Ferfitchkin joked about it just now. But where am I going to find pistols? Nonsense! I’ll draw my salary in advance and buy some. What about powder and bullets? My second will see to those. How can we arrange everything by dawn? Where do I find a second? I have no friends. Nonsense!” I cried, working myself up further and further. “It doesn’t matter! The first person I meet in the street has a duty to act as my second, just as he would have to pull a drowning man from the water. The strangest things can happen. Even if I asked the director himself tomorrow, he would have to agree out of chivalry alone, and he would have to keep the secret! Anton Antonitch....”
The truth is that at that very instant I saw the disgusting absurdity of my scheme, and the other side of the whole affair, more clearly and vividly than anyone else on earth possibly could. But ....
“Faster, driver, faster, you scoundrel, keep moving!”
“Ugh, sir!” answered the son of toil.

Suddenly a cold shudder ran through me. Wouldn’t it be better ... simply to go home? My God, my God! Why had I invited myself to this dinner yesterday? No, though, impossible. What about those three hours pacing from table to stove? No: they must pay for that pacing, they and nobody else! They must erase this disgrace! Keep driving!

Suppose they have me arrested? They wouldn’t dare! They’ll fear the scandal. Suppose Zverkov despises me so much that he refuses a duel? He certainly will; but then I’ll show them ... Tomorrow I’ll turn up at the posting station as he’s leaving, grab him by the leg, pull his coat off as he climbs into the carriage. I’ll sink my teeth into his hand and bite him. “Look what you can force a desperate man to do!” He may hit my head, and the others may batter me from behind. I’ll shout to the gathered crowd: “Look at this young puppy, going off to charm the Circassian girls after allowing me to spit in his face!”

Of course, after that it will all be finished! The office will have disappeared from the face of the earth. They’ll arrest me, try me, dismiss me from the service, imprison me, send me to Siberia. Never mind! Fifteen years later, when I come out of prison, I’ll trudge off to find him, a beggar dressed in rags. I’ll track him down in some provincial town, married and happy, with a grown-up daughter.... I’ll tell him: “Look at my sunken cheeks, my rags, you monster! I’ve lost everything: career, happiness, art, science, _the woman I loved_, all because of you. Here are the pistols. I’ve come to fire mine and ... and I ... forgive you. Then I’ll shoot into the air, and he’ll never hear of me again....”

I was actually close to tears, though at that very moment I knew perfectly well I had borrowed all this from Pushkin’s _Silvio_ and Lermontov’s _Masquerade_. Suddenly a horrible shame overcame me. I was so ashamed that I stopped the horse, climbed out of the sledge, and stood motionless in the snow in the middle of the street. The driver sighed and stared at me in amazement.

What could I do? I couldn’t continue there: that was obviously idiotic. Yet I couldn’t leave matters as they were, because that would look as though ... Heavens, how could I let it stand! After insults like those! “No!” I shouted, flinging myself back into the sledge. “It’s ordained! It’s fate! Drive on, keep driving!”
Impatiently, I punched the driver in the back of his neck.
“What are you doing? Why are you hitting me?” the peasant shouted. But he lashed his nag into such a pace that it began kicking.

Wet snow fell in huge flakes. I unbuttoned my clothes without caring. I forgot everything else: I had finally decided to deliver the slap, and felt with horror that it would happen _now, this instant_, that _no power could prevent it_. In the deserted street the lamps glowed sullenly through the snowy darkness, like funeral torches. Snow blew beneath my overcoat, beneath my coat, under my cravat, and melted. I made no attempt to wrap myself up. Everything was lost in any case.

At last we got there. Almost unconscious, I leapt out, ran up the steps, and began pounding and kicking the door. I felt terribly weak, especially in my knees and legs. The door opened quickly, as though they had been expecting me. In fact Simonov had warned them that another gentleman might arrive; this was a place where advance notice and certain precautions were necessary. It was one of those “millinery establishments” the police abolished a long time ago. During the day it really was a shop. At night, with an introduction, one could visit for other purposes.

I hurried through the dark shop into the familiar drawing room, where a single candle burned, and stopped in astonishment: nobody was there. “Where have they gone?” I asked someone. By then, of course, they had all separated. Before me stood a person wearing a stupid smile: the “madam” herself, who had seen me on previous visits. A minute later a door opened and someone else entered.

Oblivious to everything, I strode round the room, apparently talking to myself. I felt rescued from death, and a joyful awareness of it spread through my whole body. I would have delivered that slap; I certainly, certainly would! But now they weren’t here, and ... everything had disappeared, everything had changed! I looked around. I still couldn’t grasp what state I was in. Mechanically I glanced at the girl who had entered. I caught sight of a fresh, young, rather pale face, straight dark eyebrows, and serious eyes with an almost wondering expression. They attracted me immediately; if she had been smiling, I would have hated her. I began studying her more closely, with a kind of effort. My thoughts still hadn’t come together. Her face had something simple and kindly about it, but also something strangely grave. I’m sure that seriousness counted against her here, and none of those fools had noticed her. She wasn’t what you would call beautiful, however, though she was tall, looked strong, and had a good figure. Her clothes were very plain. Something disgusting stirred inside me. I walked straight up to her.

I happened to catch sight of myself in the mirror. My tormented face seemed utterly revolting: pale, angry, servile, with hair in disorder. “Never mind; I’m glad,” I thought. “I’m pleased that she’ll find me repulsive. I like the idea.”
