chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 6
paragraphs: ... Somewhere behind a screen a clock started wheezing, as though something weighed on it, as though someone were choking it. The wheezing went on unnaturally long. Then came a shrill, unpleasant chime, startlingly quick, like someone suddenly leaping forward. It struck two. I woke, though I hadn’t really been asleep; I had been lying there half-conscious.

The narrow, cramped room was almost entirely dark. Its ceiling was low, and an enormous wardrobe, stacks of cardboard boxes, and every kind of finery and rubbish cluttered it. The stub of candle burning on the table was dying, giving an occasional feeble flicker. In another few minutes the darkness would be complete.

I recovered myself quickly. Everything returned to me at once, effortlessly, as if it had been lying in ambush, waiting to spring on me again. Even while I lay unconscious, one point seemed to remain unforgotten in my memory, and my dreams circled drearily round it. Strangely, though, now that I had woken, everything that happened that day seemed part of a far, far distant past, something I had lived through and got beyond long, long ago.

My head was thick with fumes. Something seemed to hover above me, stirring me, exciting me, making me restless. Misery and malice were rising inside me again, searching for a way out. Suddenly I noticed two wide-open eyes beside me, studying me with persistent curiosity. Their expression was coolly detached, gloomy, somehow utterly distant. It weighed on me.

A grim thought entered my mind and spread through my body as a horrible sensation, like entering a damp, mouldy cellar. There was something unnatural about those eyes beginning to examine me only now. I also remembered that in the past two hours I hadn’t said one word to this creature, and had considered speech completely unnecessary. Indeed, for some reason I had enjoyed the silence. Now I suddenly grasped, with vivid clarity, the hideous idea of vice—repulsive as a spider—which, without love, crudely and shamelessly begins with the very act in which real love finds its fulfilment. We stared at one another like that for a long time. She neither lowered her eyes before mine nor changed her expression, until at last I grew uncomfortable.
“What’s your name?” I asked sharply, simply to put a stop to it.
“Liza,” she replied almost under her breath, but with no particular friendliness, and looked away.
I said nothing.
“This weather! All that snow ... disgusting!” I said almost to myself, slipping an arm despondently beneath my head and staring up at the ceiling.
She didn’t reply. It was dreadful.
“Have you lived in Petersburg all your life?” I asked after a minute, almost angrily, turning my head a little towards her.
“No.”
“Where did you come from, then?”
“Riga,” she said, plainly reluctant to answer.
“Are you German, then?”
“No. I’m Russian.”
“How long have you been here?”
“Where?”
“Here, in this house?”
“Two weeks.”
Her answers grew increasingly broken and abrupt. The candle died, and I could no longer make out her face.
“Do you have a mother and father?”
“Yes ... no ... yes, I have.”
“Where do they live?”
“Back there ... in Riga.”
“What do they do?”
“Oh, nothing.”
“Nothing? What class do they belong to?”
“Tradespeople.”
“Did you always live at home with them?”
“Yes.”
“What age are you?”
“Twenty.”
“What made you leave them?”
“Oh, no particular reason.”
Her answer meant: “Leave me alone. I feel sick and sad.”
Neither of us spoke.

God knows why I stayed. I felt increasingly sick and miserable. Without any effort or wish of mine, confused images of the previous day started flitting through my memory. Suddenly I remembered something I had seen that morning while hurrying anxiously to the office.
“Yesterday I saw some people carrying out a coffin. They almost dropped it,” I suddenly said aloud, not because I wanted to begin a conversation, but almost by accident.
“A coffin?”
“Yes, at the Haymarket. They were carrying it up from a cellar.”
“Out of a cellar?”
“Not exactly a cellar, a basement. You know ... down below ... from a house of ill-fame. Filth everywhere ... eggshells, rubbish ... a terrible smell. It was disgusting.”
Silence.
“An unpleasant day for a burial,” I began, merely to break the silence.
“What’s unpleasant about it?”
“All the snow, the damp.” I yawned.
“What difference does it make?” she suddenly said after a short pause.
“No, it’s dreadful.” I yawned again. “The gravediggers must have cursed, getting soaked with snow. And there must have been water down in the grave.”
“Why would the grave have water in it?” she asked with a kind of curiosity, though her voice was even harsher and more abrupt than before.
Suddenly I felt irritation rising in me.
“Well, there must have been a foot of water at the bottom. At Volkovo Cemetery you can’t dig a grave that’s dry.”
“Why?”
“Why? Because the ground is waterlogged, practically a swamp. They bury people in water there. I’ve seen it myself ... plenty of times.”
(In fact I had never seen it, not once; I had never even visited Volkovo. I had only heard stories about it.)
“Are you saying you don’t care how you end up dying?”
“Why would I die, though?” she replied, as if defending herself.
“Well, one day you will, and you’ll die exactly like that dead woman. She was ... a girl like yourself. She died of consumption.”
“A wench would have gone to hospital to die ...” (She already knows the whole business: she called her a “wench,” not a “girl.”)

“She owed her madam money,” I answered, growing more irritated as we argued. “So she kept earning for her right to the end, even with consumption. Some sledge-drivers nearby were telling a few soldiers about her. They must have known her. They were laughing. They’d arranged to meet in a drinking den and drink to her memory.”
I had invented much of that. A silence followed, a deep silence. She lay without moving.
“Is dying in a hospital any better, then?”
“Isn’t it all the same? Anyway, why should I die?” she added angrily.
“Not now, perhaps, but a little later.”
“Why would I die later?”
“Why indeed? You’re young now, pretty and fresh, so you command a good price. Another year of this life, though, and you’ll be quite different. Your looks will fade.”
“In one year?”

“You’ll certainly be worth less in a year,” I went on spitefully. “You’ll leave here for another house, a worse one; a year after that, a third. Down and down you’ll go, until in seven years you end up in a Haymarket basement. That’s if you’re lucky. It’ll be much worse if you catch something, consumption, for example ... and get a chill, or something of that sort. With the way you live, recovering from illness isn’t easy. Once you catch something, you may never shake it off. Then you’ll die.”
“Well, let me die, then,” she replied with downright spite, making a sudden movement.
“But you feel sorry.”
“Sorry for who?”
“For life.” No answer.
“Were you ever engaged to someone? Tell me?”
“What’s it to you?”
“Oh, I’m not interrogating you. It’s no business of mine. Why are you so angry? Naturally you may have had troubles of your own. What do they matter to me? I simply felt sorry.”
“Sorry for who?”
“For you, Liza.”
“Don’t bother,” she whispered so quietly I could barely hear, and shifted slightly again.
That infuriated me at once. What! I was being so gentle, and she....
“Do you actually believe you’re going the right way in life?”
“I don’t think about anything.”
“That’s the trouble: you don’t think. Understand your situation while there’s time. There is still time. You’re still young and attractive; you could love someone, marry, be happy....”
“Married women aren’t all happy,” she snapped in the same rude, abrupt voice she had used at first.

“Not all, naturally, but it’s better than this life in any case. Infinitely better. Besides, with love you can live even without happiness. Life is sweet even in sorrow; it’s sweet however you live. But here, what do you have except ... filth? Ugh!”

I turned away in disgust. My arguments were no longer cold calculations; I began feeling what I said and warming to my subject. Already I longed to explain the cherished ideas I had brooded over in my corner. Suddenly something blazed up inside me. I had found a purpose.

“Never mind that I’m here myself. Don’t take me as an example. Perhaps I’m worse than you. I was drunk when I arrived, though,” I quickly added in my own defence. “Besides, a man isn’t an example for a woman. The situations are different. I can degrade and dirty myself, but I’m nobody’s slave. I come, I leave, and that’s over. I shake it off and become another man. You, though, are a slave from the beginning. Yes, a slave! You surrender everything, all your freedom. Later, if you want to break the chains, you won’t be able to: the trap will hold you tighter and tighter. It’s a cursed bondage. I know it. I won’t mention anything else—you might not understand—but tell me, surely you owe your madam money? There, you see,” I added, although she hadn’t answered and was only listening silently, completely absorbed, “that’s bondage for you! You’ll never buy yourself free. They’ll make sure of that. It’s like selling your soul to the devil.... And besides ... perhaps I’m just as unfortunate myself—what do you know about it?—and deliberately roll in the mud because I’m miserable. Men take to drink out of grief, you know. Perhaps grief brought me here. Come, tell me: what good is there here? You and I ... came together ... just now, without speaking a word to each other the whole time. Only afterwards did you stare at me like a wild creature, and I at you. Is that love? Is that how one human being ought to encounter another? It’s hideous, that’s what!”
“Yes!” she agreed, abruptly and quickly.

The speed of that “Yes” positively astonished me. Perhaps the same thought had crossed her mind while she was staring at me a moment before. So she too could think certain thoughts? “Damn it, this is interesting; we have something in common!” I thought, almost rubbing my hands. And how easy it is to turn a young soul like hers!
What attracted me above everything was the chance to exercise power.
She brought her head closer to me. In the darkness I thought she had propped herself on one arm. Perhaps she was examining me. How I wished I could see her eyes. I could hear her breathing deeply.
“What brought you to this place?” I asked, already letting authority enter my voice.
“Oh, I couldn’t say.”
“Wouldn’t it be lovely to live in your father’s house! Warmth, freedom, a home that belongs to you.”
“And if home is worse than here?”

“I must find the right tone,” flashed through my mind. “Sentimentality may get me nowhere.” But the thought lasted only a moment. I swear she really interested me. Besides, I was exhausted and unsettled. And feeling so easily goes together with cunning.

“Who says that can’t happen!” I hurried to reply. “Anything is possible. I’m sure someone has wronged you, that you’re more sinned against than sinning. Of course I don’t know your story, but a girl like you probably didn’t come here because she wanted to....”
“A girl like me?” she breathed, almost inaudibly; but I caught the words.
Damn it, I was flattering her. Disgusting. Then again, perhaps it was for the best.... She said nothing.

“Listen, Liza, I’ll tell you something about myself. If I’d had a home as a child, I wouldn’t be the person I am today. I often think that. However bad things are at home, those people are your mother and father, not enemies, not strangers. At least once a year they’ll show they love you. In any case you know you’re at home. I grew up without one. Perhaps that’s why I’ve become so ... unfeeling.”
I paused again. “Maybe she doesn’t understand,” I thought. “And really, it’s absurd: I’m preaching morals.”
“If I had children, I think I’d love a daughter more than my sons, honestly,” I began indirectly, pretending to change the subject to distract her. I must admit that I blushed.
“Why would you?” she asked.
Ah! She was listening after all!

“I don’t know, Liza. I knew a father, a stern, severe man, who would get on his knees before his daughter and kiss her hands and feet. He couldn’t do enough for her, truly. At parties, while she danced, he would stand for five hours straight just watching. He was crazy about her; I understand that! At night, when she fell asleep exhausted, he would wake to kiss her in her sleep and make the sign of the cross over her. He wore a dirty old coat and was stingy with everyone else, but he’d spend his last penny on her, buying costly presents. Nothing delighted him more than seeing her pleased with his gifts. Fathers always love daughters more than mothers do. Some girls are so happy at home! I don’t think I’d ever allow my daughters to marry.”
“What next?” she asked, smiling a little.

“I’d be jealous, I really would. Imagine her kissing someone else! Loving a stranger more than her father! It hurts even to think of it. Of course that’s all nonsense; every father has to see reason eventually. But before I agreed to her marriage I think I’d worry myself to death, find something wrong with every suitor. In the end, though, I’d let her marry the man she loved. You know, the man a daughter loves always seems the worst possible choice to her father. It’s always like that. So many family troubles begin there.”
“Some fathers are happy to sell their daughters instead of giving them an honourable marriage.”
Ah, so that explained it!

“That happens, Liza, in those cursed families where there is neither God nor love,” I replied heatedly. “And without love there’s no sense either. Families like that do exist, yes, but I’m not talking about them. If you speak that way, you must have seen wickedness in your own family. You really must have been unfortunate. H’m! ... Poverty is usually behind that sort of thing.”
“Are the gentry any better? Even among poor people, aren’t there honest ones who live happily?”

“H’m ... yes. Perhaps. There’s something else, Liza: people love adding up their troubles, but they don’t count their joys. If they counted properly, they’d see that every life has its fair share of happiness. Suppose everything goes well in a family, suppose God blesses it, suppose your husband is a good man who loves you, cherishes you, never leaves you! A family like that has happiness! Sometimes happiness exists even in sorrow, and sorrow is everywhere, after all. Marry, and _you’ll find out for yourself_. Just think of the early years of marriage to someone you love: how happy they can be, how happy! And that’s quite ordinary, really. In those first days even quarrelling with your husband ends happily. Some women start quarrels with their husbands precisely because they love them. I knew a woman like that: she seemed to be saying, because she loved him she would torment him and make him feel it. You can deliberately torment someone out of love, you know. Women especially do that, thinking, ‘I’ll love him so much, make such a fuss of him afterwards, that it’s no sin to torment him a little now.’ Everyone in the house delights in seeing you; you’re happy, cheerful, peaceful, respectable.... Then there are jealous women. If their husband goes anywhere—I knew one like that—she can’t control herself; she jumps up at night and secretly runs out to find where he is, whether he’s with another woman. That’s a pity. She knows herself it’s wrong; her heart sinks and she suffers, but she loves him, and love is behind it all. How sweet it is to make peace afterwards, to admit she was wrong or forgive him! Suddenly both are so happy, as though they’ve just met, just married again, as though their love has started anew. And nobody, nobody should know what happens between husband and wife when they love each other. Whatever quarrels they have, they shouldn’t bring in even their own mother to judge or tell tales about each other. They must judge for themselves. Love is a sacred mystery; whatever happens, it should stay hidden from everyone else’s eyes. That makes it more sacred, better. They respect each other more, and so much rests on respect. If love existed once, if they married for love, why must it disappear? Surely it can be preserved! Only rarely is that impossible. If the husband is kind and honest, why shouldn’t love endure? The first stage of married love will pass, yes, but a better love will follow: their souls will be united, everything shared, no secrets between them. Once children come, even the hardest times will seem happy, provided they have love and courage. Work itself becomes a joy; you can deny yourself bread for your children and find joy even in that. Later they’ll love you for it, so you’re saving for your future. As they grow, you feel yourself an example and a support to them. Even after your death they will preserve your thoughts and feelings, because they received them from you; they’ll bear your image and likeness. You see what a great duty that is. How could it fail to bring their father and mother closer? People call having children a trial. Who says so? It’s heavenly happiness! Do you like little children, Liza? I love them terribly. You know—a rosy little boy at your breast. What husband’s heart wouldn’t soften at seeing his wife nursing their child! A plump, rosy baby, stretching and snuggling, with chubby hands and feet and clean little fingernails so tiny you laugh just looking at them; eyes that seem to understand everything. While he feeds, he holds your breast with his little hand and plays. When his father comes over, he pulls away, throws himself backwards, looks at his father and laughs as if it were wonderfully funny, then starts sucking again. Or when his little teeth come through, he bites his mother’s breast, looking sideways at her as if to say, ‘Look, I’m biting!’ Isn’t that happiness, the three together: husband, wife, child? For the sake of moments like those, you can forgive so much. Yes, Liza, you have to learn how to live yourself before blaming other people!”

“Pictures, that’s the way to reach you, pictures like these,” I thought, although I really had been speaking with feeling. Suddenly I went crimson. “What if she bursts out laughing now? What would I do?” The thought enraged me. By the end of my speech I had become truly excited, and now somehow my vanity was hurt. The silence went on. I almost nudged her.

“Why do you—” she began, then stopped. But I understood. Something different trembled in her voice, something soft and embarrassed instead of the old harsh, abrupt resistance. It was so embarrassed that I suddenly felt ashamed and guilty myself.
“What is it?” I asked with gentle curiosity.
“Well, you...”
“What?”
“Well, you ... you sound just like a book somehow,” she said, and a note of irony had returned to her voice.
Her words sent a stab through my heart. They were nothing like what I had expected.

I didn’t understand that she was concealing her feelings behind irony. That is often the last refuge of modest people with a chaste soul when someone clumsily forces his way into their private feelings. Pride makes them resist surrender until the last possible moment and shrink from revealing their emotions to you. I should have understood from the timid way she had repeatedly approached her sarcastic remark, finally forcing herself to say it with an effort. But I understood nothing, and a malicious feeling took possession of me.
“Just you wait!” I thought.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 7
paragraphs: “Oh, stop that, Liza! How can you say I sound like a book when even I, a stranger, feel sick about this? Though I don’t see it as a stranger, really; it cuts me to the heart.... Can you possibly, can you possibly not feel sick at being here yourself? Habit evidently works wonders! God knows what habit can do to a person. Do you seriously imagine you’ll never age, that you’ll always be pretty, that they’ll keep you here for ever and ever? I’m not even speaking of the disgusting life here.... Though let me say this about it—about the life you’re living now. You’re young, attractive, pleasant, with a soul and feelings; yet as soon as I recovered my senses just now I felt sick to be here with you! You can only come to a place like this drunk. If you were somewhere else, though, living as decent people live, perhaps you would do more than attract me. I might fall in love with you, be grateful for a glance, never mind a word. I might linger outside your door, kneel before you, think of you as my promised bride and count it an honour to be allowed to. I wouldn’t dare think anything impure about you. Here, though, I know I need only whistle, and you must come with me whether you wish to or not. I don’t consider your wishes; you have to consider mine. Even the lowest labourer hires out his work without enslaving his whole self; besides, he knows he’ll be free again before long. When are you free? Just think what you’re surrendering here. What part of yourself are you making a slave of? Your soul as well as your body. You’re selling a soul you have no right to sell! You hand over your love for every drunkard to abuse! Love! You know, that’s everything: a priceless diamond, a maiden’s treasure. A man would give his soul, face death itself, to win that love. What is yours worth now? You’re sold completely, body and soul; nobody needs to strive for love when he can have everything without it. There’s no greater insult to a girl, do you understand? I’ve heard, of course, how they console you poor fools: they allow you lovers of your own. But that’s a farce, a pretence, a way of laughing at you, and you fall for it! Do you believe your lover really loves you? I don’t. How can he, knowing you may be summoned away from him at any moment? He would be a vile fellow if he did! Would he have the slightest respect for you? What do you share? He laughs at you and robs you; that’s the whole of his love! You’re fortunate if he doesn’t beat you. Very likely he does that too. If you have a lover, ask whether he’ll marry you. He’ll laugh in your face, unless he spits in it or hits you, though he may not be worth a bad halfpenny himself. Think about it: what have you destroyed your life for? The coffee they give you, the plentiful food? What are they fattening you up for? An honest girl couldn’t swallow that food, knowing why she was being fed. You owe money here; naturally you’ll always owe it, right to the end, until the visitors start despising you. That will happen soon, too. Don’t count on your youth: here it rushes past like an express train. They’ll throw you out. And it won’t be just that. Long before then she’ll begin nagging, scolding, abusing you, as though you hadn’t sacrificed your health for her, hadn’t thrown away your youth and your soul for her profit, but had ruined her, reduced her to poverty, stolen from her. Don’t imagine anyone will defend you. The others, your companions, will turn on you too, to gain her favour. Everyone here is a slave; they lost their conscience and their pity long ago. They’ve become utterly vile, and nothing on earth is viler, more disgusting, more insulting than their abuse. Here you surrender everything without conditions: youth, health, beauty, hope. At twenty-two you’ll look thirty-five; you’ll be lucky not to be diseased. Pray to God for that! No doubt you think you have fun here and no work to do! But there is no harder or more dreadful work in the world; there never has been. You’d think the tears alone would wear your heart out. When they drive you away, you won’t dare say a word, even half a word. You’ll leave as though it were your fault. You’ll move to another house, then a third, then somewhere else, until finally you sink to the Haymarket. There you’ll get beaten at every turn; that’s considered good manners. The visitors there don’t know how to be friendly without hitting you. You don’t believe it’s so horrible? Go and look sometime, see for yourself. Once, on New Year’s Day, I saw a woman outside a doorway. They had thrown her out as a joke, to let her feel the frost because she’d been crying so much, and locked the door behind her. At nine in the morning she was already completely drunk, half-naked, dishevelled, covered in bruises. Powder covered her face, but she had a black eye, and blood ran from her nose and teeth: a cabman had just beaten her. She sat on the stone steps holding some kind of salted fish, crying, wailing about her luck, banging the fish against the steps. Cabmen and drunken soldiers crowded the doorway and jeered. You don’t believe you’ll ever become that? I’d hate to believe it too. But how can you know? Perhaps ten years ago, eight years ago, that same woman with the fish came here fresh as a cherub, innocent and pure, ignorant of evil, blushing at every word. Perhaps she resembled you: proud, easily offended, different from the rest. Perhaps she looked like a queen and knew what happiness awaited the man who loved her and whom she loved. You see how it ended? And suppose at that very moment, drunk and dishevelled, beating that fish against the filthy steps—suppose just then she remembered her innocent early days in her father’s house? Going to school, the neighbour’s boy waiting along the road, declaring he would love her all his life and devote himself to her; the two of them promising to love for ever and marry as soon as they grew up! No, Liza, you’d be fortunate to die soon of consumption in some corner, some basement, like the woman I mentioned. In hospital, you say? You’ll be lucky if they admit you. What if your madam still finds you useful here? Consumption is a strange disease, unlike fever. A sufferer hopes until the very last moment and insists he’s all right. He deceives himself, and that suits your madam perfectly. Don’t doubt it: that’s how things stand. You’ve sold your soul, and on top of that you owe money, so you dare not speak. But when you’re dying, everyone will abandon you and turn away, because nothing more can be got out of you. Worse, they’ll reproach you for taking up room, for taking so long to die. Beg as much as you like; you won’t get a drink of water without abuse: ‘When are you finally going, you filthy hussy? Your moaning keeps us awake; you make the gentlemen sick.’ It’s true; I’ve heard such words myself. They’ll shove you into the dirtiest corner of the basement to die, in the damp and darkness. What will you think, lying there alone? When you’re dead, strangers’ hands will lay you out, grumbling and impatient. Nobody will bless you or sigh for you. They’ll only want you gone as quickly as possible. They’ll buy a coffin, carry you to the grave like that poor woman today, and celebrate your memory in the tavern. In the grave there’ll be sleet, filth, wet snow; no need to trouble themselves over you. ‘Lower her down, Vanuha. Just her luck: even here the hussy goes head first. Shorten that rope, you scoundrel.’ ‘She’s fine as she is.’ ‘Fine, is she? She’s on her side! She was a fellow human being, after all! Oh, never mind, shovel the earth over her.’ They won’t want to spend much time arguing about you. They’ll throw in the wet blue clay as fast as possible and head for the tavern.... That will be the end of your memory on earth. Other women have children to visit their graves, fathers, husbands. For you, no tears, no sighs, no remembrance. Nobody in the whole world will ever visit. Your name will disappear from the earth as though you had never existed, never been born! Nothing but mud and filth, however hard you knock on the coffin lid at night when the dead rise, however you cry, ‘Let me out, good people, let me live in daylight! My life wasn’t a life at all; it was thrown away like a dishcloth, drunk away in a Haymarket tavern. Let me out, good people, let me live in the world again.’”

I worked myself into such a state that a lump formed in my own throat, and ... and suddenly I stopped. I sat up in alarm, bent over anxiously, and listened, my heart pounding. There was reason enough for me to be alarmed.

For some time I had sensed that I was overturning her soul, tearing her heart apart. And—and the more certain I became, the more eagerly I wanted to reach my goal, as quickly and completely as possible. The display of my skill swept me along; yet it wasn’t merely a game....

I knew my speech was stiff, artificial, even bookish. In fact I couldn’t speak except “like a book.” That didn’t worry me. I knew, I felt, that she would understand, and that the very bookishness might help me. But now, with my intended effect achieved, panic suddenly seized me. I had never seen despair like this! She lay face down, her face driven into the pillow, gripping it in both hands. Her heart was breaking. Her young body shook all over as if in convulsions. Stifled sobs tore through her chest, suddenly bursting into weeping and wailing; then she pressed herself harder into the pillow. She didn’t want anyone here, not a single living soul, to know of her anguish or her tears. She bit the pillow and her hand until it bled—I saw that later—or dug her fingers into her tangled hair and went rigid with the effort to restrain herself, holding her breath and clenching her teeth. I started saying something, asking her to calm down, but felt I had no right to dare. Suddenly, shivering coldly, almost terrified, I began fumbling in the dark, hurriedly trying to dress and leave. In the darkness, despite all my efforts, I couldn’t dress quickly. Then my hands found a matchbox and a candlestick holding a whole candle. The instant I lit the room, Liza sprang up, sitting upright in bed, and stared at me almost without comprehension, her face distorted by a half-mad smile. I sat beside her and took her hands. She recovered herself and moved impulsively towards me, about to seize hold of me, but didn’t dare; slowly she bent her head before me.
“Liza, my dear, I was wrong ... forgive me, my dear,” I began. But her fingers tightened so painfully round my hand that I realised I was saying the wrong thing, and stopped.
“Here’s my address, Liza. Come and see me.”
“I’ll come,” she replied firmly, keeping her head bent down.
“But I have to go now. Goodbye ... until we see each other again.”

I stood up, and so did she. Suddenly she blushed all over, shuddered, snatched a shawl from a chair, and wrapped it round herself up to her chin. While doing so she gave another sickly smile, blushed again, and looked at me strangely. I felt miserable. I wanted to leave quickly, to disappear.

“Wait a moment,” she suddenly said in the passage, just by the doorway, stopping me with a hand on my overcoat. She hastily put the candle down and ran off. Evidently she had remembered something, or wanted to show me something. As she ran, her face flushed, her eyes shone, and a smile appeared on her lips. What did it mean? Reluctantly I waited. A minute later she returned, looking as if she were asking forgiveness for something. It was no longer the same face, the same expression as earlier that evening: gloomy, suspicious, stubborn. Now her eyes were pleading and gentle, yet also trusting, affectionate, timid. Children look that way at someone they love very much when asking a favour. Her eyes were light hazel, beautiful eyes, alive with feeling, capable of expressing love as well as sullen hatred.

Without explaining anything, as though I were some higher being who must understand without explanations, she offered me a piece of paper. At that moment her whole face shone with innocent, almost childish triumph. I unfolded it. A medical student, or someone like that, had written her a love letter: very grand and flowery, but extremely respectful. I can’t remember its words now, but I remember clearly the genuine feeling visible beneath the lofty phrases, feeling impossible to counterfeit. When I finished reading, I found her bright, questioning, childishly impatient eyes fixed on me. She watched my face intently, eager to hear what I would say. In a few hurried words, with a sort of pride and joy, she explained that she had attended a dance in a private home. The family were “very nice people, _who knew nothing_, absolutely nothing, because she had only arrived here so recently, and everything had happened ... and she hadn’t decided to stay, and would certainly leave as soon as she paid her debt...” The student had been at that party and danced with her all evening. They talked, and it turned out he had known her in Riga as a child; they had played together, a very long time ago. He knew her parents. But he knew nothing _about this_, nothing whatsoever, and suspected nothing! The day after the dance, three days earlier, he had sent the letter through the friend who had accompanied her to the party ... and ... well, that was everything.
When she finished speaking, she lowered her shining eyes in a kind of shy embarrassment.

The poor girl treasured that student’s letter, and had hurried off to fetch her one precious possession because she didn’t want me to leave without knowing that she too was honestly, sincerely loved, that someone addressed her respectfully too. No doubt the letter was destined to remain in her box and lead nowhere. All the same, I’m certain she would preserve it all her life as a treasure, her pride and her justification. Now, at such a moment, she had remembered it and brought it out with innocent pride to improve my opinion of her, so that I might see, so that I too might think well of her. I said nothing, squeezed her hand, and left. How desperately I wanted to get away.... I walked the whole way home, although melting snow still fell in heavy flakes. Exhausted, shattered, bewildered, I went on. But behind my bewilderment the truth was already beginning to shine through. The disgusting truth.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 8
paragraphs: It took me a while, however, to agree to acknowledge that truth. In the morning, after a few hours of heavy, leaden sleep, I woke and immediately remembered everything that had happened the day before. My _sentimentality_ with Liza the previous night positively astonished me—all those “outcries of horror and pity.” “Imagine having such an attack of womanish hysteria, ugh!” I concluded. And why had I forced my address on her? Suppose she came? Well, let her; it didn’t matter.... But _obviously_ that wasn’t the main or most pressing business now. I had to hurry, at any cost, to restore my reputation with Zverkov and Simonov as soon as possible. That was what mattered. That morning I was so absorbed in it that I actually forgot Liza altogether.

First I had to return the money borrowed from Simonov the previous day, without delay. I decided on a desperate step: ask Anton Antonitch for fifteen roubles outright. Luckily he was in an excellent mood that morning and gave me the money immediately, at the first request. This delighted me so much that, while signing the IOU with a swagger, I casually mentioned that the night before “I’d been celebrating with friends at the Hôtel de Paris. We were giving a comrade a farewell party—really, you might call him a childhood friend. You know the sort: an outrageous rake, terribly spoiled, but from a good family of course, considerable money, a brilliant career. Witty, charming, a regular Lovelace, you understand. We drank an extra ‘half-dozen’ and ...”
It all went beautifully. I delivered the whole thing easily, naturally, and with complete self-satisfaction.
As soon as I got home, I wrote to Simonov.

Even now, remembering my letter’s truly gentlemanly, cheerful, open tone fills me with admiration. Tactfully, politely, and above all without any unnecessary words, I accepted the blame for everything. In my defence—“if I may really be permitted to defend myself”—I claimed that, being quite unused to wine, I had become drunk on my first glass. I said I had drunk it before their arrival, while waiting at the Hôtel de Paris between five and six. I apologised especially to Simonov and asked him to pass my explanation to the rest, particularly Zverkov, whom “I seemed to remember, as if in a dream,” having insulted. I added that I would have visited each of them myself, but my head hurt, and besides I couldn’t face them. I was particularly pleased by the light, almost casual touch in my style—always strictly polite, of course. Better than any argument, it immediately showed them that I took a rather independent view of “last night’s unpleasant business.” I wasn’t remotely as crushed as you, my friends, probably supposed; on the contrary, I regarded the episode with the calm self-respect proper to a gentleman. “On a young hero’s past no censure is cast!”

“There’s a positively aristocratic playfulness to it!” I thought admiringly, rereading the letter. “All because I’m an intellectual, a cultivated man! Someone else in my position wouldn’t have known how to escape, but here I am, out of it and cheerful again, entirely because I’m ‘a cultivated and educated man of our day.’ And perhaps yesterday’s business really was all caused by wine. H’m!” ... No, it wasn’t the wine. While waiting from five to six I hadn’t drunk a thing. I had lied to Simonov, lied shamelessly; and I still felt no shame.... Oh, hang it, the important thing was that I had got rid of the affair.

I enclosed six roubles, sealed the letter, and asked Apollon to deliver it to Simonov. Hearing that it contained money, Apollon became more respectful and agreed. Towards evening I went for a walk. Yesterday had left my head still aching and dizzy. But as evening advanced and the twilight thickened, my impressions changed and grew confused, with my thoughts following them. Something inside me wasn’t dead; deep in my heart and conscience it refused to die, expressing itself as acute depression. Mostly I pushed through the busiest commercial streets, along Myeshtchansky Street, along Sadovy Street, and through Yusupov Garden. I had always particularly enjoyed wandering those streets at dusk, just when crowds of every sort of working person headed home from the day’s work, their faces sour with worry. That cheap bustle, that unadorned prose of life, was exactly what appealed to me. But this time the crowds irritated me more than ever. I couldn’t understand what was wrong, couldn’t discover the explanation. Something kept painfully rising in my soul, refusing to settle. I reached home completely upset, as if some crime lay on my conscience.

The possibility of Liza’s coming troubled me constantly. It seemed strange that, among all yesterday’s memories, this one should torment me particularly, almost on its own. By evening I had successfully forgotten everything else, dismissed it all, and remained perfectly pleased with my letter to Simonov. But I felt no satisfaction on this point. It was as though Liza alone worried me. “What if she comes?” I kept thinking. “Well, what does it matter? Let her come! H’m! It’s horrible, though, to think of her seeing how I live. Yesterday I appeared such a hero; now, h’m! It’s horrible how I’ve let myself go. The room looks like a beggar’s. And I actually went out to dinner in clothes like those! My American leather sofa, with the stuffing poking out. My dressing gown, too ragged to cover me. She’ll see all that, and Apollon too. The beast will certainly insult her. He’ll use her as a way of being rude to me. Naturally I’ll panic as usual, bow and scrape before her, clutch the dressing gown round myself, start smiling and lying. Oh, how beastly! But the beastliness isn’t even the worst of it! There’s something more serious, more disgusting, more vile! Yes, viler! And I’ll have to put that dishonest, lying mask on again! ...”
The moment my thoughts reached that point, I flared up in anger.

“Why dishonest? What was dishonest about it? I spoke sincerely last night. I remember having real feelings too. I wanted to awaken an honourable feeling in her.... It was good that she cried; it will do her good.”

Still I couldn’t settle. Throughout the evening, even after I had returned home, even after nine, when I reckoned Liza couldn’t possibly come any more, she haunted me. Worse, I always remembered her in the same position. One moment from the whole night stood vividly in my imagination: when I struck the match and saw her pale, twisted face, with its tortured expression. What a pitiful, unnatural, distorted smile she had then! But I didn’t know that fifteen years later I would still see Liza in my imagination, always wearing that same pitiful, distorted, inappropriate smile from that instant.

The next day I was again ready to dismiss everything as nonsense, the product of overexcited nerves, and above all _exaggeration_. I always knew about that weakness in myself, and sometimes feared it intensely. “I exaggerate everything; that’s my mistake,” I told myself hourly. Yet every train of thought ended with the same refrain: “Liza will probably come anyway.” My anxiety sometimes drove me into a rage. “She’ll come, she’s bound to come!” I shouted, running round the room. “If not today, then tomorrow. She’ll find me out! The cursed romanticism of these pure hearts! Oh, the vileness, the silliness, the stupidity of these ‘miserable sentimental souls!’ How can they fail to understand? How could anyone fail to understand? ...”
At that point, though, I stopped abruptly, thoroughly confused.

And how few words, I thought in passing, how very few had been needed. A little idyll—an affected, artificial, bookish idyll at that—had been enough to turn a whole human life instantly in the direction I wished. That’s virginity for you! Fresh, untouched soil!

Sometimes I thought of visiting her, “telling her everything,” and begging her not to come. But the thought filled me with such rage that, had that “damned” Liza been beside me then, I believe I would have crushed her. I would have insulted her, spat at her, driven her out, hit her!

One day passed, however, then another, then another. She didn’t come, and I began to calm down. After nine o’clock I felt particularly cheerful and bold; sometimes I even began dreaming rather sweet dreams. I became Liza’s salvation, for instance, merely because she came to me and I talked to her.... I develop her mind, educate her. Eventually I notice she loves me, loves me passionately. I pretend I haven’t understood—though I don’t know why I pretend, perhaps simply for effect. Finally, confused, transformed, trembling, sobbing, she throws herself at my feet and tells me I have saved her, that she loves me more than anything in the world. I am astonished, but.... “Liza,” I say, “do you suppose I failed to notice your love? I saw it, guessed everything, but I didn’t dare approach you first. I had influence over you and feared you might force yourself, out of gratitude, to return my love, might try to awaken a feeling that perhaps wasn’t in your heart. I didn’t want that ... it would have been tyranny ... it would have been indelicate.” In short, at this point I launch into European subtleties of inexplicable loftiness, à la George Sand. “But now, now you belong to me, you are my creation, you are pure and good, you are my noble wife.
‘Into my house come bold and free, Its rightful mistress there to be’.”
Then we live together, travel abroad, and so on, and so on. Eventually even I found the whole thing vulgar and began sticking my tongue out at myself.

Besides, they wouldn’t let her out, “the hussy!” I thought. They’re reluctant to let the girls leave, especially in the evening—for some reason I imagined she would come in the evening, at seven precisely. Still, she had said she wasn’t completely enslaved there yet and retained certain rights; so, h’m! Damn it, she’ll come, she’s certain to come!

It was fortunate, really, that Apollon’s insolence distracted me at that time. He drove me beyond the limit of my patience! He was the plague of my life, the curse Providence had inflicted on me. For years we had quarrelled constantly, and I hated him. My God, how I hated him! I don’t believe I ever hated another person so much, especially at certain moments. He was an elderly, dignified man who worked part-time as a tailor. For some mysterious reason he despised me without limit and looked down on me intolerably. In fact, he looked down on everyone. One glance at his smoothly brushed flaxen head, the tuft he combed up over his forehead and greased with sunflower oil, or his dignified mouth compressed into a V, told you that here stood a man who never doubted himself. He was a pedant in the most extreme degree, the greatest pedant I ever met on earth, with vanity worthy of Alexander of Macedon. He adored every button on his coat, every fingernail, absolutely adored them, and you could see it! Towards me he behaved like a complete tyrant. He rarely spoke; when he happened to look my way, his firm, majestic, self-assured and invariably ironic gaze sometimes drove me to fury. He performed his duties as if granting me an immense favour, though he did next to nothing and didn't actually consider himself obliged to do anything. He unquestionably thought me the world's greatest fool. The only reason he “didn’t get rid of me” was that he could collect wages every month. For seven roubles a month he consented to do nothing for me. The suffering he caused me ought to earn forgiveness for many of my sins. My hatred became so strong that sometimes the sound of his footsteps nearly sent me into convulsions. I particularly loathed his lisp. His tongue must have been too long, or something of that kind: he lisped constantly and seemed very proud of it, imagining it greatly enhanced his dignity. He spoke slowly, deliberately, hands behind his back, eyes on the floor. What especially maddened me was hearing him read the psalms aloud to himself behind his partition. Many battles I fought over that reading! But he loved reading aloud in the evening, in a slow, steady singsong, as though reading over the dead. Interestingly, that is how he has ended up: hiring himself out to read psalms over the dead, while also killing rats and making blacking. At that time, though, I couldn’t get rid of him. He seemed chemically fused with my existence. Besides, nothing could have persuaded him to agree to leave. Furnished lodgings were impossible for me: my rooms were my private solitude, my shell, my cave, where I hid from all humanity. For some reason Apollon seemed an inseparable part of that flat, and for seven years I couldn’t dismiss him.

Paying his wages two or three days late, for example, was impossible. He would have made such a fuss that I’d have had nowhere to hide. But in those days I was so angry with everyone that, for some reason and with some purpose, I decided to _punish_ Apollon by withholding the wages due to him for two weeks. I had been planning this for a long time, for the past two years, simply to teach him not to put on airs with me, and to prove that I could withhold his pay if I chose. I meant to say nothing about it, and deliberately kept silent, to defeat his pride and make him mention his wages first. Then I would take seven roubles from a drawer and show him that I had the money specially set aside, but wouldn’t, wouldn’t, simply wouldn’t pay. I wouldn’t because “that’s my wish,” because “I’m the master and I decide,” because he had been disrespectful and rude. But if he asked politely, I might soften and give it to him; otherwise he could wait another fortnight, another three weeks, a whole month....

Angry as I was, he defeated me nevertheless. I couldn’t last four days. He began as he always did in such situations: they had happened before; I had made earlier attempts. And please note that I knew it all in advance, knew his nasty tactics by heart. He would start with an exceptionally stern stare, holding it for several minutes, particularly when meeting me or seeing me out. If I resisted and pretended not to notice, he proceeded, still silently, to further tortures. Suddenly, _à propos_ of nothing, he would glide softly into my room while I read or paced, stand in the doorway with one hand behind his back and one foot behind the other, and fix me with a stare beyond sternness, a stare of complete contempt. If I abruptly asked what he wanted, he wouldn’t answer. He would keep staring for several seconds, then press his lips together in a peculiar way and, with a deeply significant air, deliberately turn and deliberately return to his room. Two hours later he would emerge and present himself again in exactly the same manner. Sometimes in my fury I didn’t even ask what he wanted. I simply lifted my head sharply, imperiously, and stared back. We would look at one another for two minutes; finally he turned with slow dignity and withdrew for another two hours.

If this still failed to bring me to reason and I continued my rebellion, he would begin sighing as he looked at me: long, deep sighs, as if measuring the depth of my moral collapse. Naturally it always ended in his complete victory. I raged and shouted, but still had to do what he wanted.
This time the familiar staring campaign had barely started before I lost control and flew at him in fury. Even without him, my irritation was already unbearable.

“Wait,” I shouted wildly as he slowly, silently turned towards his room, one hand behind his back. “Wait! Come back, come back, I’m telling you!” I must have roared in such an extraordinary way that he turned and even looked at me with some surprise. But he still refused to speak, which infuriated me.
“How dare you come in and stare at me like that when I haven’t called you? Answer me!”
He regarded me calmly for thirty seconds, then started turning away again.
“Stop!” I roared, rushing towards him. “Don’t move! There. Now tell me: what did you come in here to stare at?”

“If you have an order for me, carrying it out is my duty,” he replied after another pause. He lisped slowly and evenly, raising his eyebrows and calmly turning his head from side to side, all with maddening composure.

“That isn’t what I asked, you torturer!” I shouted, scarlet with anger. “I’ll tell you myself why you came. You see I haven’t paid your wages, and you’re too proud to bow down and ask. So you punish me with those stupid stares, torment me, without the faint-est idea how stupid it is—stupid, stupid, stupid, stupid! ...”
He would have turned away without speaking again, but I grabbed him.

“Listen,” I shouted. “There’s the money. Can you see? Here it is.” I took it from the table drawer. “All seven roubles, but you won’t get them. You ... will ... not ... get ... them until you come humbly, with your head bowed, and beg my forgiveness. Do you understand?”
“That is impossible,” he replied with the most extraordinary self-assurance.
“That’s what will happen,” I said. “On my word of honour, that’s what will happen!”

“And I have nothing to ask forgiveness for,” he continued, as if my outbursts hadn’t reached him. “Besides, you called me a ‘torturer.’ I could have you summoned to the police station for insulting behaviour whenever I choose.”
“Go ahead, summon me,” I roared. “Do it now, this minute, this second! You’re a torturer just the same! A torturer!”
He merely looked at me, then turned. Ignoring my loud calls, he walked evenly back to his room without once looking round.
“Without Liza, none of this would have happened,” I concluded inwardly. A minute later I went behind his screen myself, with a solemn, dignified air, although my heart was beating slowly and heavily.
“Apollon,” I said quietly and emphatically, despite being out of breath, “go and fetch the police officer immediately. Don’t delay a minute.”
Meanwhile he had settled at his table, put on his spectacles, and picked up his sewing. When he heard my command, he burst into a loud laugh.
“Now, this very minute! Go, or you have no idea what will happen to you.”

“You’re certainly out of your mind,” he remarked without even lifting his head, lisping as deliberately as ever as he threaded his needle. “Whoever heard of someone calling the police on himself? And as for being frightened, you’re getting upset for nothing. Nothing will come of it.”
“Go!” I shrieked, seizing his shoulder. I felt that in another moment I would hit him.

But I failed to notice the door from the passage opening slowly and quietly just then. A figure entered, stopped, and stared at us in bewilderment. I looked over, nearly fainted with shame, and rushed back to my room. Grasping my hair with both hands, I pressed my head against the wall and stood there motionless.

Two minutes later came Apollon’s measured footsteps. “Some woman has come to see you,” he said, eyeing me with peculiar severity. He stepped aside and admitted Liza, but refused to leave, standing there watching us sarcastically.
“Go away, get out,” I ordered desperately. Just then my clock started whirring and wheezing, and struck seven.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 9
paragraphs: “Into my house come bold and free, Its rightful mistress there to be.”

I stood in front of her, crushed, dejected, and disgustingly embarrassed. I believe I even smiled while trying desperately to cover myself with the skirts of my ragged, padded dressing gown, exactly as I had imagined the scene during my recent fit of depression. Apollon stood over us for a couple of minutes, then left, but that brought me no relief. Worse, she too was terribly embarrassed, more than I would have expected. At the sight of me, naturally.

“Sit down,” I said automatically, pulling a chair up to the table and seating myself on the sofa. She immediately obeyed and looked at me with wide eyes, clearly expecting something from me straight away. That innocent expectation infuriated me, but I held myself in check.
She should have pretended not to notice anything, behaved as though all were normal. Instead she ... and I felt dimly that I would make her pay dearly for _every bit of this_.

“You’ve caught me in a strange situation, Liza,” I began, stammering and knowing this was the wrong beginning. “No, no, don’t think anything,” I cried when I saw her suddenly blush. “I’m not ashamed of being poor.... Quite the opposite: I’m proud of my poverty. Poor but honourable.... A person can be both poor and honourable,” I muttered. “Anyway ... would you care for some tea?....”
“No,” she started to say.
“Just a moment.”
I sprang up and ran to Apollon. Somehow I had to escape from the room.

“Apollon,” I whispered with feverish urgency, throwing down the seven roubles I had kept clenched in my fist all this time, “here are your wages. Look, I’m paying you. But now you must help me: bring tea and a dozen rusks from the restaurant. If you refuse, you’ll make me miserable! You don’t understand who this woman is.... This is—everything! Perhaps you imagine something.... But you have no idea who that woman is! ...”

Apollon had already resumed his work and put his spectacles back on. At first he gave the money a sideways glance without speaking or putting down his needle. Then, paying no attention to me and making no reply, he continued fiddling with the needle, which he still hadn’t threaded. For three minutes I waited before him, arms folded _à la Napoléon_. Sweat dampened my temples; I could feel how pale I was. But thank God, the sight must have stirred his pity. Once the needle was threaded he rose deliberately, pushed his chair back deliberately, took off his glasses deliberately, counted the money deliberately, and finally asked over his shoulder, “A whole portion?” Then he deliberately left the room. As I returned to Liza, a thought struck me: why not run away just as I was, in my dressing gown, anywhere at all, and let whatever happened happen?
I sat back down. She watched me anxiously. Neither of us spoke for several minutes.
“I’ll kill him,” I suddenly shouted, banging my fist on the table so hard that ink splashed from the inkstand.
“What are you saying!” she exclaimed, giving a start.

“I’ll kill him! Kill him!” I shrieked, suddenly pounding the table in utter frenzy, while perfectly aware how stupid that frenzy was. “You don’t understand, Liza, what that torturer means in my life. He tortures me.... He’s gone to get some rusks now; he ...”
Suddenly I started crying. It was an attack of hysteria. Even as I sobbed I felt terribly ashamed, yet I couldn’t stop the tears.
She looked frightened.
“What’s happened? What’s the matter?” she cried, anxiously fussing round me.

“Water. Bring me some water, over there!” I murmured weakly, although inside I knew perfectly well I could manage without water and without a weak voice. I was, as people say, _putting it on_, trying to save appearances, even though the attack itself was real.

She brought water and looked at me in bewilderment. Just then Apollon arrived with the tea. After everything that had happened, this ordinary, prosaic tea suddenly seemed horribly petty and undignified, and I turned scarlet. Liza looked positively frightened of Apollon. He left without glancing at either of us.
“Liza, do you think me contemptible?” I asked, staring straight at her, trembling with impatience to discover what was in her mind.
She was embarrassed and had no idea how to reply.

“Drink your tea,” I said angrily. My anger was directed at myself, but naturally she would pay for it. Suddenly a dreadful hatred of her rose in my heart; I think I could have killed her. To punish her I silently vowed not to speak another word throughout her visit. “She’s responsible for all of it,” I thought.

We stayed silent for five minutes. The tea sat untouched on the table. I was now deliberately refusing to begin, to make her still more uncomfortable; she couldn’t easily start drinking alone. Several times she looked at me with sad bewilderment. I stubbornly said nothing. Of course I suffered most myself, fully aware of the disgusting pettiness of my spiteful stupidity, yet unable to control myself all the same.

“I want to ... leave ... that place for good,” she began, simply to break the silence somehow. Poor girl: that was precisely what she shouldn’t have mentioned at such a stupid moment to such a stupid man. Her tactless, unnecessary openness made my heart ache with pity. But something hideous instantly choked all compassion and provoked still greater malice. I no longer cared what happened. Five more minutes went by.
“Perhaps I’m disturbing you,” she began timidly, almost inaudibly, and started to rise.
But the instant I saw that first movement of wounded dignity, I actually shook with malice and immediately burst out.

“Tell me, please: why did you come here?” I began, breathless, not caring whether my words followed logically. I wanted everything out at once, in one explosion; I didn’t even trouble about how to start. “Why have you come? Answer me, answer,” I cried, scarcely aware of what I was doing. “I’ll tell you why, my good girl. You came because I spoke all that sentimental nonsense to you then. Now you’ve melted like butter and want another helping of fine feelings. Well, you should know I was laughing at you then. And I’m laughing at you now. Why are you trembling? Yes, I was laughing at you! Just before that, at dinner, the men who came earlier that evening had insulted me. I came to your place to beat one of them, an officer. But it didn’t work: I couldn’t find him. I had to avenge the insult on somebody, get something of my own back. You happened to be there, so I took my anger out on you and laughed at you. I’d been humiliated, so I wanted to humiliate someone. They’d treated me like a rag, so I wanted to exercise power.... That’s all it was. And you imagined I had come specially to save you. Didn’t you? Is that what you imagined? Is it?”

I knew she might be confused and fail to follow every detail, but I also knew she would understand the essential point very well indeed. And she did. Her face became white as a handkerchief. She tried to speak, her lips struggling painfully, but collapsed into a chair as if an axe had struck her down. From then on she listened with parted lips and staring eyes, shuddering in dreadful fear. The cynicism, the cynicism of my words crushed her....

“Save you!” I continued, leaping from my chair and running up and down in front of her. “Save you from what? Perhaps I’m worse than you myself. Why didn’t you throw it back in my face while I preached: ‘What did you come here for yourself, then? To give us a sermon?’ Power, that’s what I wanted, power. I wanted amusement. I wanted to squeeze tears out of you, humiliation, hysteria. That was what I wanted! Of course I couldn’t sustain it, being the miserable creature I am. I got frightened and, the devil knows why, foolishly gave you my address. Afterwards, before I even reached home, I was cursing and swearing at you because of that address. I already hated you for the lies I’d told you. Because I only like playing with words, dreaming; what I really want, you know, is for all of you to go to hell. That’s my real wish. I want peace. Yes, I’d sell the whole world for a farthing this instant, provided I could be left in peace. Should the world collapse, or should I miss my tea? Let the world collapse, I say, as long as I always get my tea. Did you know that? Well, anyway, I know I’m a blackguard, a scoundrel, an egoist, a sluggard. For three days I’ve been shuddering at the thought of your visit. And do you know what has worried me most throughout those three days? I posed as such a hero before you; now you’d see me in a miserable torn dressing gown, beggarly and disgusting. I just told you I wasn’t ashamed of my poverty. Well, I am ashamed of it, more ashamed than of anything else. I fear it more than I would fear being exposed as a thief, because my vanity is like skin flayed off: even a breath of air hurts. By now you must surely understand that I’ll never forgive you for finding me in this wretched dressing gown, snapping at Apollon like a vicious little dog. The saviour, the former hero, was snarling like a mangy, unkempt sheepdog at his servant, while the servant mocked him! I’ll never forgive you for those tears I couldn’t stop shedding in front of you just now, like some foolish woman shamed into crying! Nor will I ever forgive you for this confession I’m making now! Yes, you must pay for everything: because you appeared like this, because I’m a blackguard, because I’m the nastiest, stupidest, most ridiculous and most envious worm on earth. The others are no better, yet the devil knows why they’re never embarrassed, whereas every louse will always insult me; that’s my fate! What do I care if you don’t understand a word of it! What do I care about you, what do I care whether you’re ruined in that place or not? Do you understand? How I’ll hate you after saying this, hate you for being here and hearing it. A man scarcely speaks this openly once in his life, and then only in hysterics! ... What else do you want? Why are you still standing before me after all that? Why are you tormenting me? Why won’t you leave?”

But something strange happened then. I was so used to thinking and imagining through books, to picturing everything in the world exactly as I had invented it beforehand in my dreams, that I couldn’t immediately grasp this strange development. What happened was this: Liza, whom I had insulted and crushed, understood far more than I supposed. From everything I said she understood what a woman understands first when she truly loves: that I was unhappy myself.

The fear and hurt in her face first gave way to sorrowful bewilderment. As I called myself a scoundrel and a blackguard, with tears streaming down—I cried throughout the entire tirade—her whole face began twitching. She almost rose to stop me. When I finished, she paid no attention to my shouts of “Why are you here? Why don’t you leave?” She understood only how bitter it must have been for me to say those things. Besides, the poor girl was so crushed and considered herself so infinitely beneath me: how could she feel anger or resentment? Suddenly an irresistible impulse made her leap from the chair and reach towards me, holding out her hands, still timid, still not daring to move.... My heart too changed at that moment. Then she abruptly rushed forward, flung her arms round me, and burst into tears. I could no longer restrain myself either; I sobbed as I had never sobbed before.

“They won’t let me ... I can’t be good!” I managed to say. Then I went to the sofa, collapsed face down, and sobbed for fifteen minutes in genuine hysteria. She came beside me, put her arms round me, and stayed still like that. The trouble was, though, that hysteria couldn’t last for ever. And—I am writing the disgusting truth—as I lay face down, my face pressed into the nasty leather pillow, I gradually became aware of a distant feeling, involuntary but irresistible, that it would be awkward now to lift my head and look Liza in the eyes. Why did I feel ashamed? I don’t know, but I did. Another thought entered my overstrained mind: our roles had completely reversed. She was the heroine now, and I was only a crushed, humiliated creature, just as she had been before me that night, four days earlier.... All these thoughts came while I lay on the sofa with my face hidden.
My God! Surely I wasn’t jealous of her at that moment.

I don’t know; even today I can’t decide. Naturally I understood my own feelings even less at the time than I do now. I can’t live without dominating and tyrannising over someone, but ... reasoning explains none of this, so reasoning is useless.

Still, I forced myself to raise my head; sooner or later I had to.... To this day I’m convinced that it was precisely my shame at looking at her that suddenly kindled another feeling, setting my heart aflame: the desire to master and possess her. Passion shone in my eyes, and I seized her hands tightly. How I hated her, and how strongly she attracted me at that instant! Each feeling strengthened the other. It was almost an act of revenge. Astonishment, even terror, appeared in her face at first, but only for a moment. Then she embraced me warmly, ecstatically.

chapters.title: Part 2, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Fifteen minutes later I was hurrying round the room in frantic impatience, going every minute to the screen to peer through a crack at Liza. She sat on the floor with her head against the bed, probably crying. But she wouldn’t leave, and that irritated me. This time she understood everything. I had delivered the final insult, but ... no need to describe it. She realised that my passionate outburst had been nothing but revenge, another humiliation, and that my earlier, almost groundless hatred had now acquired a _personal hatred_, born of envy.... I don’t insist that she understood all this clearly. But she certainly understood completely that I was contemptible and, worse, incapable of loving her.

I know people will tell me this is unbelievable. But being as malicious and stupid as I was is itself unbelievable. Perhaps they will add that it was strange I didn’t love her, or at least value her love. Why strange? To begin with, by then I couldn’t love. I repeat: for me, loving meant tyranny, demonstrating my moral superiority. All my life I have been unable to imagine love in any other form. These days I sometimes go so far as to think that love really is the right, freely granted by the beloved, to tyrannise over her.

Even in my underground dreams, love was always a struggle. I invariably began with hatred and ended by subduing the other person morally; afterwards I never knew what to do with the person I had subdued. Why should that surprise anyone? I had corrupted myself so thoroughly, become so detached from “real life,” that I had actually thought of reproaching her, shaming her for coming to hear “fine sentiments.” It never even occurred to me that she hadn’t come for fine sentiments at all, but to love me. For a woman, every reformation, every rescue from ruin, every moral renewal is contained in love and can express itself only through love.

Yet as I ran about the room and peered through the crack in the screen, I didn’t hate her so intensely. Her presence simply weighed on me unbearably. I wanted her gone. I wanted “peace,” to be alone again in my underground world. Real life, with its unfamiliarity, pressed on me so heavily I could hardly breathe.

Several minutes passed, but she stayed motionless, as if unconscious. I was shameless enough to tap lightly on the screen, as though reminding her.... She started, jumped up, and rushed to find her kerchief, hat, and coat, as if escaping from me.... Two minutes later she emerged and looked at me with heavy eyes. I gave her a malicious grin, though I forced it in order to _keep up appearances_, then turned away from her gaze.
“Goodbye,” she said as she moved towards the door.
I hurried over, caught her hand, opened it, pushed something into it, and closed it again. Then I immediately turned and rushed to the far corner of the room, to avoid seeing, at any rate....

A moment ago I intended to lie: to write that I did it by accident, without knowing what I was doing, out of foolishness, because I had lost my head. But I don’t want to lie, so I’ll state it plainly: I opened her hand and put the money into it ... out of spite. The idea occurred while I was pacing and she sat behind the screen. One thing, though, I can say with certainty. Deliberate as that cruelty was, it didn’t come from my heart; it came from my evil mind. It was so artificial, so consciously invented, so completely a product of intellect and books, that I couldn’t maintain it for even a minute. First I rushed away to avoid looking at her; then, ashamed and desperate, I rushed after her. I opened the door into the passage and listened.
“Liza! Liza!” I called down the stairs, but in a quiet, hesitant voice, without any boldness. Nobody answered. I thought I could hear her footsteps farther down.
“Liza!” I called again, louder now.
Still no reply. But just then the stiff glass outer door creaked heavily open and slammed shut, the sound echoing up the stairwell.
She was gone. Hesitantly I returned to my room, weighed down by a horrible feeling.

I stopped beside the table and the chair where she had sat, and stared blankly ahead. A minute passed; suddenly I started. There on the table, directly before me, I saw.... In short, I saw a crumpled blue five-rouble note, the one I had pushed into her hand a moment earlier. It was the very same note: there couldn’t be another, none existed in the flat. So when I dashed to the far corner, she had managed to throw it out of her hand onto the table.

Well! I should have expected her to do that. Should I have expected it? No: I was so selfish, with so little respect for other human beings, that I couldn’t even imagine such a response. I couldn’t bear it. A minute later I rushed like a madman to get dressed, threw on whatever came to hand, and ran headlong after her. She couldn’t have gone two hundred paces by the time I reached the street.

The night was still. Snow fell in heavy masses, almost straight down, covering the pavement and the empty roadway as though with a pillow. Nobody was out in the street; there wasn’t a sound anywhere. The streetlamps cast a forlorn, useless glimmer. I ran two hundred paces to the crossroads and stopped dead.
Where had she gone? And why was I chasing after her?

Why? To fall at her feet, sob with remorse, kiss them, beg her forgiveness! I longed to do it; my whole chest seemed to be tearing apart, and never, never will I remember that moment indifferently. But what would be the point, I thought? Might I not hate her tomorrow precisely because I had kissed her feet today? Would I make her happy? Hadn’t I discovered for the hundredth time that very day what I was worth? Wouldn’t I torment her?
Standing in the snow, I stared into the troubled darkness and thought it over.

“And wouldn’t it be better?” I fancied later, back at home, smothering the living pain in my heart with fantasies. “Wouldn’t it be better if she kept the resentment of this insult for ever? Resentment is purification, a consciousness that stings and hurts most terribly! Tomorrow I would have stained her soul and worn out her heart. Now, though, the insult will remain alive inside her. However disgusting the filth that awaits her, the sense of being insulted will raise and purify her ... through hatred ... h’m! ... perhaps through forgiveness too.... But will any of that make things easier for her? ...”
And here I will ask an idle question on my own behalf: which is better, cheap happiness or exalted suffering? Well, which one is better?

Those were my dreams as I sat at home that evening, almost dying from the pain in my soul. Never had I suffered such remorse and anguish. Yet when I rushed out of my rooms, could there have been the slightest doubt I would turn back halfway? I never saw Liza again and have heard nothing about her. I should add that for a long time afterwards I remained pleased with my phrase about the benefits of resentment and hatred, although misery had almost made me ill.

Even now, so many years later, there is something terribly evil about the memory. I have many evil memories these days, but ... wouldn’t it be better to end my “Notes” here? I think beginning them was a mistake. At any rate, I’ve felt ashamed throughout the writing of this story. It is less literature than a corrective punishment. Long accounts of how I ruined my life—rotting morally in my corner, lacking a suitable environment, cut off from real life, nursing rancour in my underground world—certainly wouldn’t be interesting. A novel requires a hero, whereas here I have _deliberately_ assembled every characteristic of an anti-hero. Above all, the result is unpleasant, because we are all cut off from life, all crippled, every one of us, to some degree. We are so detached that real life immediately provokes something like disgust; we can’t bear being reminded of it. We have almost come to regard real life as a task, as hard labour, and privately we all agree that it is better in books. Then why do we sometimes fret and rage? Why behave perversely and demand something else? We don’t know what we want ourselves. If those petulant prayers were answered, we would be worse off. Try it: give any of us a little extra independence, for instance; free our hands, broaden the scope of our activity, loosen the control, and we ... yes, I assure you ... we would immediately beg to be controlled again. I know that will probably anger you, and you’ll begin shouting and stamping. Speak for yourself, you’ll say, and for your misery in your underground holes; don’t dare include us all. Excuse me, gentlemen: that “all of us” isn’t my excuse. In my own life I have merely taken to an extreme what you haven’t dared take even halfway. What’s more, you have mistaken your cowardice for good sense and comforted yourselves with self-deception. Perhaps, after all, there is more life in me than in you. Look at it more carefully! We no longer even know what living means, what it is, what to call it. Leave us alone without books and immediately we’ll be lost and bewildered. We won’t know what to attach ourselves to, what to hold on to, what to love or hate, what to respect or despise. Being human oppresses us: being individual human beings of real flesh and blood. We’re ashamed of it, regard it as disgraceful, and try to become some impossible, generalised human being instead. We are stillborn. For generations our fathers have not been living men, and we like that better and better; we’re acquiring a taste for it. Soon we’ll find some way of being born from an idea. But enough. I don’t want to write any more from “Underground.”
[The notes of this paradoxalist continue beyond this point. He couldn't stop himself from writing more, but we think we may bring them to an end here.]
